+q, +q, +q, +q, +q, +q on a hexagon

quiz.q: A short dipole has p = 2 × 10⁻⁹ C m. What is the potential on its axis 0.3 m away (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses r³ (field formula) instead of r²

quiz.q: For the same dipole, what is the potential at the same distance on the equatorial plane (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Halves the axial value as for the field

quiz.q: Six charges of +1 nC each sit at the corners of a regular hexagon of side 0.1 m. What is the potential at the centre (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Each corner is 0.1 m from the centre (hexagon side = circumradius). V = 6 × 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹/0.1 = 540 V.
quiz.mistake: Thinks symmetric charges give zero potential as they do for the field

quiz.q: At the same large distance, how does the dipole potential at θ = 60° compare with that on the axis (θ = 0°)?
quiz.explain: V ∝ cos θ: cos 60° = 0.5 compared with cos 0° = 1.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin θ instead of cos θ

quiz.q: The potential of a dipole at an axial distance r is V. What is it at 2r on the axis?
quiz.explain: Dipole potential ∝ 1/r²: (1/2)² = 1/4.

quiz.q: Charges +3 nC, -5 nC and +8 nC sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle; the centroid is 0.15 m from each. What is V at the centroid (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign of the -5 nC charge

quiz.q: Why is it often easier to find the potential than the field due to several charges?
options: Potential does not depend on distance
Potential is a scalar, so contributions add algebraically
quiz.explain: No directions or components are needed for a scalar sum.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): At points on the equatorial plane of a dipole, the potential is zero but the field is not. Reason (R): Potential is a scalar sum, while the field is a vector sum. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite potentials cancel as numbers; the fields' components along the axis add instead of cancelling.
quiz.mistake: Assumes zero potential means zero field

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'On the dipole's middle line, potential is zero. So there's no field there either?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Zero potential, but the vector fields add up along -p. Potential and field are different things!
teach.nudge: Good! Is potential a vector or a scalar? What about the field?

learn.hook: Contour lines on a hill map join points of equal height. Bunched-up contours mean a steep slope. Equipotential surfaces do the same for electric fields.
points: An equipotential surface has the same potential at every point, so no work is done in moving a charge along it.
The electric field is always normal to equipotential surfaces (otherwise a component along the surface would do work).
Shapes: concentric spheres for a point charge, parallel planes perpendicular to a uniform field; distorted shapes for a dipole and for two like charges.
E = -dV/dl: the field points in the direction of steepest decrease of potential, with magnitude |ΔV|/Δl measured normal to the equipotentials.
Closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field; widely spaced ones mean a weak field.

example.q: Two equipotential planes 5 cm apart differ by 10 V. Find E.
steps: = 200 V m⁻¹, from the higher to the lower potential

learn.reallife: Survey of India's topographic maps show height contours; electrical engineers draw equipotential maps around substations to keep 'step voltage' safe for people walking nearby.

games.title: Equipotential truths
items: No work is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface.
ΔV = 0, so W = qΔV = 0.
The electric field can be parallel to an equipotential surface.
E is always perpendicular to it.
E points in the direction in which potential increases fastest.
E points towards decreasing potential.
Two different equipotential surfaces can intersect.
That point would have two potentials.
The unit V m⁻¹ is the same as N C⁻¹.
Both are units of electric field.

quiz.q: Equipotentials are 2 cm apart and differ by 4 V each in a uniform field. What is the field strength (in V m⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert cm to m

quiz.q: How much work is done in moving a 5 µC charge 3 m along an equipotential surface at 100 V (in J)?
quiz.explain: ΔV = 0 along an equipotential, so W = 0.

quiz.q: The equipotential surfaces of an isolated point charge are
options: concentric spheres centred on the charge
quiz.explain: V = kQ/r is constant where r is constant.

quiz.q: In a region, V changes from 30 V to 10 V over 4 mm along x. What is the field along x (in V m⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Ex = -dV/dx = -(10 - 30)/0.004 = +5000 V m⁻¹. The field points towards lower potential (+x).
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign of E = -dV/dx

quiz.q: Why must the electric field be perpendicular to an equipotential surface?
options: If E had a component along the surface, moving a charge along it would need work, contradicting constant V
Because the surface is a conductor
quiz.explain: Zero work along the surface means zero field component along it.
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason based on shape instead of work

quiz.q: In the region where equipotentials are drawn closer together, the field is
quiz.explain: E = ΔV/Δl; smaller Δl for the same ΔV gives larger E.

quiz.q: For a uniform field along +x, the equipotential surfaces are
options: planes parallel to the y-z plane
planes parallel to the x-y plane
quiz.explain: They must be perpendicular to E, i.e., perpendicular to x.
quiz.mistake: Places planes parallel to the field

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Two equipotential surfaces never intersect. Reason (R): At an intersection point, the potential would have two different values. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Potential at a point has a single value, so two different equipotentials cannot share a point.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the reason to the assertion

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Which way does the electric field point compared to equipotential surfaces?'
teach.praise: Chirp! E is normal to equipotentials, pointing from high to low potential. And no work along them!
teach.nudge: Close! Think about the work done along an equipotential. What does that say about E's direction?

topics.title: Potential energy of a system of charges

learn.hook: To pack charges into a tiny space you must fight their repulsion. That fight stores energy, like compressing a spring, and nuclear fission later releases it.
points: Two charges: U = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r₁₂) = kq₁q₂/r₁₂, the work needed to assemble them from infinity.
Like charges: U > 0 (work must be done to push them together). Unlike charges: U < 0 (they attract, so work is released).
Three or more charges: add U for every pair, U = k(q₁q₂/r₁₂ + q₁q₃/r₁₃ + q₂q₃/r₂₃).
Work by an external agent to change a configuration = U(final) - U(initial).
Four charges at the corners of a square have six pairs: four sides and two diagonals.

example.q: Find the work needed to place three charges of 1 µC each at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.1 m.

learn.reallife: Inside a uranium nucleus in a reactor at Kudankulam or Tarapur, protons are packed so tightly that their Coulomb potential energy is enormous. When the nucleus splits, part of that energy is released.

items.q: Pairs among 3 charges
Pairs among 4 charges
Pairs among 5 charges
Sign of U for +q and -q
Sign of U for -q and -q
U for two 1 µC charges 9 m apart (in mJ)

games.title: Energy of assembly
items: The potential energy of two unlike charges is negative.
q₁q₂ < 0.
The potential energy of a system of charges depends on the order in which they are brought in.
U depends only on the final positions.
For three charges, U is the sum over three pairs.
Pairs 12, 13 and 23.
Bringing two like charges closer increases U.
U = kq₁q₂/r grows as r shrinks.
A negative U means that the system was assembled with work done on it.
Negative U means energy was released; work must be supplied to separate them.

quiz.q: What is the potential energy of two charges of +2 µC and +3 µC placed 0.6 m apart (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Divides by r² as for force

quiz.q: A proton and an electron are 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. What is the sign of their electrostatic potential energy?
quiz.explain: q₁q₂ = (+e)(-e) < 0, so U < 0: the system is bound.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the signs of the charges

quiz.q: Four charges of +1 µC each are at the corners of a square of side 0.3 m. How many pairs must be counted in the total potential energy?
quiz.explain: 4C2 = 6 pairs: four sides and two diagonals.

quiz.q: Charges +4 µC and -2 µC are 0.2 m apart. How much work is needed to separate them to infinity (in J)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sign and gives -0.36 J

quiz.q: Two equal charges of 1 µC are moved from 0.3 m apart to 0.1 m apart. What work is done by the external agent (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: U changes from 0.03 J to 0.09 J, so W = 0.09 - 0.03 = 0.06 J.

quiz.q: Charges +q, +q and -q sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. What is the total potential energy?
quiz.explain: Pairs: (+q,+q) gives +kq²/a; two (+q,-q) pairs give -2kq²/a. Total = -kq²/a.
quiz.mistake: Counts all pairs with the same sign

quiz.q: The potential energy of a pair of charges is independent of
options: the path and order in which they were brought together
quiz.explain: U is a state function of the final configuration because the force is conservative.

quiz.q: Three charges of 2 µC each are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.3 m. What is the total potential energy (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Each pair: 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻¹²/0.3 = 0.12 J. Three pairs: 0.36 J.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know: 'How do I find the energy stored in a gang of four charges?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Add kq₁q₂/r for every pair: four charges means six pairs. Awesome!
teach.nudge: Good start! What do we calculate for each pair of charges, and then what do we do?

topics.title: Potential energy in an external field and the electron volt

learn.hook: An electron accelerated through a single volt gains a tiny 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Physicists liked that unit so much they gave it a name: the electron volt.
points: A charge q at a point where an external potential is V(r) has potential energy qV(r). The external field's sources are taken as fixed.
Electron volt: energy gained by an electron (or lost) when it moves through a potential difference of 1 V. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Also keV, MeV.
A charge q accelerated through ΔV gains kinetic energy qΔV.
Two charges q₁, q₂ in an external field: U = q₁V(r₁) + q₂V(r₂) + kq₁q₂/r₁₂. The last term is their mutual energy.
An electron (negative) gains energy moving towards higher potential; a proton gains energy moving towards lower potential.

example.q: A proton is accelerated from rest through 1000 V. Find its kinetic energy in eV and J.

learn.reallife: Old CRT televisions, still found in some Indian homes, accelerated electrons through about 20 kV, giving each one roughly 20 keV of energy before it hit the screen to make it glow.

items.text: A charge q at potential V has energy ___.
Two charges in an external field also have a mutual term kq₁q₂/___.
An electron gains kinetic energy moving towards ___ potential.
The electron volt is a unit of ___.

quiz.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. What kinetic energy does it gain (in eV)?
quiz.explain: K = eΔV = 500 eV.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the electron's small mass changes the energy

quiz.q: What is 5 MeV in joules (in units of 10⁻¹³ J)? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
An alpha particle (charge 2e) is accelerated through 2 kV. What kinetic energy does it gain (in keV)?
quiz.explain: K = qΔV = 2e × 2000 V = 4000 eV = 4 keV.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that an alpha particle carries 2e

quiz.q: A charge of 3 µC is at a point where the external potential is 400 V. What is its potential energy (in mJ)?
For two charges q₁ and q₂ in an external field, the total potential energy contains
quiz.explain: Each charge interacts with the external field, and the two also interact with each other.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out the mutual interaction term

quiz.q: Which statement is correct about an electron released from rest in an electric field?
options: It moves towards higher potential and gains kinetic energy
quiz.explain: For negative charge U = -eV falls as V rises, so it moves to higher V.
quiz.mistake: Applies the rule for positive charges to electrons

quiz.q: Two charges 5 µC and -3 µC are placed 15 cm apart, both on the V = 0 equipotential of an external field. What is the system's potential energy (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Both charges sit where the external V = 0, so only the mutual term remains: kq₁q₂/r = 9 × 10⁹ × (5 × 10⁻⁶)(-3 × 10⁻⁶)/0.15 = -0.9 J.

quiz.q: An electron volt is
options: the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V
a unit of potential equal to 1 V
the potential at 1 m from an electron
quiz.explain: eV is energy: charge e times 1 V.
quiz.mistake: Thinks eV is a unit of potential

teach.ask: Gappu sees '13.6 eV' in a book. 'Is an electron volt a kind of volt?'
teach.praise: Chirp! An eV is energy: what an electron gains across 1 volt, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good! Is the eV a unit of potential or of energy? How is it defined?

topics.title: Potential energy of a dipole in a field

learn.hook: A compass needle settles pointing north and wobbles back if nudged. A dipole in an electric field has the same favourite direction, set by its potential energy.
points: Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field: U(θ) = -pE cosθ = -p·E (taking U = 0 at θ = 90°).
θ = 0 (p along E): U = -pE, minimum, stable equilibrium.
θ = 180° (p opposite E): U = +pE, maximum, unstable equilibrium.
Work done by an external agent to rotate a dipole from θ₁ to θ₂: W = pE(cosθ₁ - cosθ₂).
Turning a dipole from stable (0°) to unstable (180°) needs W = 2pE.

example.q: A dipole p = 2 × 10⁻²⁹ C m is in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. Find the work to turn it from 0° to 90°.

learn.reallife: Liquid crystal displays in phones assembled in Noida rely on molecular dipoles: applying a field rotates them to their minimum-energy orientation, switching pixels on and off.

games.title: Stable or not?
items: A dipole aligned along the field is in stable equilibrium.
U is minimum at θ = 0.
A dipole antiparallel to the field feels a large torque.
At 180° the torque pE sinθ is zero, though equilibrium is unstable.
U = -pE cosθ.
That is the standard expression.
Work to rotate a dipole from 90° to 0° is positive.
U falls from 0 to -pE, so the external work is -pE (the field does the work).
The potential energy of a dipole is maximum at θ = 180°.
U = +pE there.

quiz.q: A dipole p = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at θ = 0° in a field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is its potential energy (in units of 10⁻⁴ J)?
How much work is needed to rotate a dipole of p = 10⁻⁸ C m from θ = 0° to 180° in a field of 5 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (in units of 10⁻⁵ J)?
In which orientation is an electric dipole in unstable equilibrium in a uniform field?
quiz.explain: At 180° torque is zero but U is maximum, so any tilt makes it rotate away.

quiz.q: A molecule with p = 10⁻²⁹ C m is turned from θ = 0° to θ = 60° in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. What work is needed (in units of 10⁻²⁴ J)?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 60° in place of cos 60°

quiz.q: The expression U = -p·E for a dipole assumes U = 0 when
quiz.explain: -pE cos 90° = 0, so the reference is θ = 90°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reference is at θ = 0

quiz.q: At which angle are both the torque and the potential energy of the dipole zero?
options: No angle: U = 0 at 90°, where the torque is maximum
quiz.explain: U = 0 at 90°, where τ = pE is maximum; τ = 0 at 0° and 180°, where U = ∓pE ≠ 0.
quiz.mistake: Assumes torque and energy vanish together

quiz.q: A dipole in a field of 10⁴ N C⁻¹ has a potential energy of -3 × 10⁻⁵ J when aligned with the field. What is p (in nC m)?
quiz.explain: U = -pE, so p = 3 × 10⁻⁵/10⁴ = 3 × 10⁻⁹ C m = 3 nC m.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the negative sign in p

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dipole placed in a uniform field tends to align with the field. Reason (R): Its potential energy is minimum when p is along E. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Systems move towards minimum potential energy; the torque rotates p into line with E.
quiz.mistake: Does not relate the torque to the energy minimum

teach.ask: Gappu tilted a dipole in a field: 'Why does it swing back to point along the field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! U = -pE cosθ is lowest at θ = 0, and the torque turns it back there. Stable!
teach.nudge: Nice! Where is the dipole's potential energy lowest, and what pushes it there?

learn.hook: Copper is full of free electrons. Put it in a field and they rush around until they have cancelled the field inside. That simple fact gives conductors five superpowers.
points: Inside a conductor (in electrostatic equilibrium) the field is zero; free charges rearrange until the internal field vanishes.
Just outside, the field is normal to the surface; a tangential part would push charges along the surface.
There is no net charge in the interior; any excess charge sits on the outer surface.
The whole conductor (inside and surface) is at one potential: it is an equipotential volume.
Just outside, E = (σ/ε₀) n̂, with σ the local surface charge density and n̂ the outward normal.

example.q: A conducting surface has σ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². Find the field just outside. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
steps: ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, normal to the surface
example.answer: ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, outward along the normal

learn.reallife: Metal cabinets of ATMs and server racks in Bengaluru data centres stay at one potential and are earthed, so stray charge never builds up across the electronics inside.

games.title: Conductor rules
items: In electrostatics, the field inside a conductor is zero.
Free charges cancel any internal field.
Excess charge on a conductor spreads evenly through its volume.
It lives on the outer surface.
Just outside a charged conductor, the field is normal to the surface.
A tangential component would move charges.
Different points on the surface of a charged conductor can be at different potentials.
The conductor is an equipotential.
The field just outside a conductor is σ/(2ε₀).
For a conductor it is σ/ε₀; σ/(2ε₀) is for a thin sheet.

games.title: How a conductor reaches equilibrium
games.prompt: Put the events in order when a conductor is placed in a field
items: External field acts on free electrons
Electrons drift opposite to the field
Charge piles up on the surfaces
Induced charges create an opposing field
Net field inside becomes zero and charges stop

quiz.q: What is the electric field inside a solid metal sphere carrying 5 µC, in electrostatic equilibrium (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: In equilibrium the field inside any conductor is zero.

quiz.q: Where does excess charge given to an isolated conductor reside?
options: Only at its sharpest point and nowhere else
quiz.explain: Gauss's law with E = 0 inside shows no charge in the interior.

quiz.q: A charged conductor has potential 200 V at its surface. What is the potential at its centre (in V)?
quiz.explain: E = 0 inside, so V does not change from surface to centre.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero field means zero potential

quiz.q: A conductor has σ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁸ C m⁻². What is the field just outside (in kN C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
Why is the electrostatic field at the surface of a conductor normal to it?
options: Any tangential component would move surface charges, so equilibrium needs it to vanish
Because the field inside is non-zero
quiz.explain: In equilibrium charges are at rest, so no force along the surface.
quiz.mistake: Gives a geometric rather than a physical reason

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential. Reason (R): The field inside and the tangential field on its surface are zero. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With no field along any path within or on the conductor, no work is done, so V is the same everywhere.
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between zero field and constant potential

quiz.q: The surface charge density at a point on a conductor is doubled. The field just outside that point
quiz.explain: E = σ/ε₀ is proportional to σ.

quiz.q: A neutral metal slab is placed in a uniform external field. Which statement is correct?
options: Negative charge appears on the face where the field enters and positive on the face where it leaves
Positive charge appears where the field enters
quiz.explain: Electrons drift against the field to the entry face; the other face is left positive. Their field cancels the external field inside.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is there no electric field inside a metal spoon kept near a charged comb?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Free electrons shift to the surface until their field cancels the outside field inside the metal. Smart!
teach.nudge: Good! What do the free electrons in the metal do when a field acts on them?

topics.title: Shielding, sharp points and charged shells

learn.hook: During a thunderstorm on the Mumbai-Pune expressway, the safest place is inside your car. The metal body acts as an electrostatic shield.
points: Electrostatic shielding: the field inside any empty cavity of a conductor is zero, whatever the outside fields or charges. Sensitive instruments are kept in metal enclosures.

Charge on a conductor concentrates where the surface is most curved (sharp points), giving large σ and large fields; air can break down there (corona discharge). Lightning conductors use sharp points.
Charge q placed inside a cavity of a neutral conducting shell induces -q on the cavity wall and +q on the outer surface.
Uniformly charged shell of radius R: V = kq/r outside (r ≥ R) and V = kq/R, constant, everywhere inside.
Inside the shell E = 0 but V is not zero; it equals the surface potential.

example.q: A shell of radius 0.1 m carries 2 nC. Find V at its centre and at 0.3 m from the centre.
example.answer: 180 V at the centre; 60 V at 0.3 m

learn.reallife: Tall buildings in Kolkata and temple towers often carry a pointed copper lightning conductor connected to an earthed plate. The point helps discharge build-up, and the conductor guides strikes safely to the ground.

games.title: Shielding facts
items: The field inside a cavity in a conductor is zero even when there are charges outside the conductor.
That is electrostatic shielding.
Charge density is greatest at the flattest part of a conductor.
It is greatest at sharp, highly curved parts.
The potential inside a charged hollow shell is zero.
It is constant and equal to kq/R.
A charge q inside a cavity induces -q on the cavity wall.
So that the field inside the conductor's material is zero.
Sitting inside a car during lightning is safer than standing in an open field.
The metal body shields the inside.

quiz.q: A thin shell of radius 0.2 m carries 4 nC. What is the potential at a point 0.1 m from its centre (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Inside the shell V is constant and equal to kq/R = 36/0.2 = 180 V.
quiz.mistake: Uses the distance from the centre instead of R, or takes V = 0 inside

quiz.q: For the same shell (4 nC, R = 0.2 m), what is the potential at 0.4 m from the centre (in V)?
quiz.explain: Outside V = kq/r = 36/0.4 = 90 V.

quiz.q: Why does a lightning conductor have pointed tips?
options: Charge density and field are very high at sharp points, so charge leaks away into the air
quiz.explain: High σ at points gives strong fields that ionise air, enabling discharge.

quiz.q: A charge +q is placed at the centre of a cavity in a neutral conducting sphere. What charges appear on the inner and outer surfaces?
options: -q on the inner surface, +q on the outer surface
quiz.explain: The inner wall gets -q so that E = 0 in the metal; the outer surface gets +q since the conductor is neutral overall.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the conductor stays neutral overall

quiz.q: Which is the best example of electrostatic shielding?
options: Keeping a sensitive instrument inside a closed metal box
Using a long copper wire as an antenna
quiz.explain: The field inside a closed conducting enclosure is zero.

quiz.q: A conducting sphere of radius 9 cm has a potential of 200 V at its surface. What is the charge on it (in nC)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses R in cm without converting

quiz.q: A hollow conducting sphere carries charge Q₁. A small charge Q₂ is placed at its centre. The field outside the sphere at distance r from the centre is
quiz.explain: The outer surface ends up with Q₁ + Q₂ (the original Q₁ plus the induced +Q₂), so Gauss's law gives k(Q₁ + Q₂)/r².
quiz.mistake: Ignores the induced charge on the outer surface

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Corona discharge is seen near sharp points of high-voltage conductors. Reason (R): Surface charge density is larger at points of smaller radius of curvature. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Large σ means large field σ/ε₀, which ionises the surrounding air.
quiz.mistake: Does not link curvature with charge density

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If lightning hits a car, why are people inside safe?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The metal body is a conducting shell: charge stays on the outside and the field inside is zero. Safe!
teach.nudge: Good! What is special about the field inside a closed conductor?

learn.hook: Put a slab of glass between charged plates and the field inside weakens. The glass has no free electrons, yet it fights back. How?
points: Dielectrics are insulators. Unlike conductors, they have no free charges, but their molecules get polarised in a field, which only partly reduces the field inside.
Polar molecules (e.g. H₂O) have permanent dipoles that align with the field; non-polar molecules get induced dipoles by charge separation.
Polarisation P = dipole moment per unit volume. For linear dielectrics P = χe E, where χe is the electric susceptibility.
A uniformly polarised slab acquires bound surface charges ±σp on its faces. These produce a field opposite to the applied one, so the field inside is reduced (not cancelled).
Contrast: inside a conductor E becomes exactly zero; inside a dielectric E is only reduced.

example.q: A slab is placed in a uniform field E₀. Its bound charges produce an opposing field of E₀/4. Find the net field inside.
steps: The dielectric reduces but does not cancel the field

learn.reallife: Mica and ceramic are used as insulating dielectrics in capacitors on the circuit boards of Indian-made smartphones and EV chargers.

games.title: Polar or non-polar dielectric molecule
items: H₂O
HCl
CO₂
O₂
N₂
NH₃

games.title: Dielectric facts
items: A dielectric placed in a field has zero field inside, like a conductor.
The field is reduced, not cancelled.
Polarisation is the dipole moment per unit volume.
That is its definition.
Non-polar molecules can become dipoles in an external field.
These are induced dipoles.
Bound surface charges on a polarised slab can flow away if touched by a wire.
Bound charges are tied to molecules; they are not free.
The field due to bound charges inside the slab opposes the applied field.
That is why the net field is reduced.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a conductor and a dielectric placed in an electric field?
options: Both make the field zero inside
A dielectric increases the field inside
The field inside a conductor becomes zero, but inside a dielectric it is only reduced
A conductor only reduces the field
quiz.explain: Free charges in a conductor cancel the field; bound charges in a dielectric only partly oppose it.
quiz.mistake: Treats a dielectric like a conductor

quiz.q: Polarisation P of a dielectric is defined as
quiz.explain: P = total dipole moment / volume.
quiz.mistake: Confuses polarisation with surface charge density

quiz.q: In the relation P = χe E, the quantity χe is called the
quiz.explain: χe measures how strongly a material polarises in response to the field.

quiz.q: A non-polar molecule placed in an electric field
options: develops an induced dipole moment along the field
gets a permanent dipole moment opposite to the field
quiz.explain: The field pushes the nucleus and electron cloud apart, inducing a dipole along E.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the molecule gains net charge

quiz.q: Why do polar molecules not show any net polarisation without an external field?
options: Their dipoles always cancel inside each molecule
Their permanent dipoles point in random directions due to thermal motion
They are all aligned opposite to each other in pairs
quiz.explain: Random orientations average out; an applied field partly aligns them.

quiz.q: A dielectric slab in an applied field E₀ has a net internal field of 0.2E₀. What field do its bound charges produce (in terms of E₀, opposing)?
quiz.explain: Net = E₀ - E_bound, so E_bound = E₀ - 0.2E₀ = 0.8E₀.
quiz.mistake: Gives the net field instead of the bound-charge field

quiz.q: Where do the bound charges of a uniformly polarised dielectric slab appear?
options: On its two faces perpendicular to the field
On the faces parallel to the field
quiz.explain: Inside, neighbouring dipole charges cancel; only the end faces have uncancelled bound charge.
quiz.mistake: Puts the bound charge in the volume

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dielectric reduces the field between capacitor plates. Reason (R): Bound charges on its surfaces produce a field opposing the applied field. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The opposing field of the induced surface charges reduces the net field.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how bound charges create an opposing field

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Glass has no free electrons. How can it weaken an electric field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The molecules become dipoles, bound surface charges appear, and their field opposes the applied one. Wow!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the molecules of glass in a field, and what charges appear on its surfaces?

learn.hook: A camera flash charges up in a second and fires its energy in a millisecond. The little device that holds that charge is a capacitor.
points: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator, carrying charges +Q and -Q.
Capacitance C = Q/V, where V is the potential difference between the plates. Unit: farad (1 F = 1 C V⁻¹). Practical units: µF (10⁻⁶ F), nF (10⁻⁹ F), pF (10⁻¹² F).
C depends only on the geometry (size, shape, separation) and the medium between the conductors, not on Q or V.
Too high a voltage makes the field exceed the dielectric strength (about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹ for air), and the medium breaks down. Circuit symbol: two parallel lines.
Parallel plate capacitor: field between the plates is σ/ε₀ (σ = Q/A) and practically zero outside, ignoring fringing at the edges.

example.q: A capacitor stores 60 µC when connected to a 12 V supply. Find C. What charge does it hold at 24 V?
steps: C does not change with V
example.answer: C = 5 µF; Q = 120 µC at 24 V

learn.reallife: The ceiling fans in most Indian homes use a 2–4 µF capacitor to help the motor start; when a fan hums but will not spin, a technician often replaces this capacitor.

games.title: Capacitance check
items: Doubling the charge on a capacitor doubles its capacitance.
C = Q/V; V also doubles, so C is unchanged.
Capacitance depends on the medium between the plates.
A dielectric increases C.
Between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor, E = σ/ε₀.
The two sheet fields add.
Outside an ideal parallel plate capacitor, E = σ/ε₀.
Outside, the fields cancel to zero.
If the voltage across a capacitor is too high, the dielectric can break down.
The field exceeds the dielectric strength.

quiz.q: A capacitor holds 40 µC at 8 V. What is its capacitance (in µF)?
A 10 µF capacitor is connected to a 9 V battery. What charge does it store (in µC)?
quiz.explain: Q = CV = 10 µF × 9 V = 90 µC.

quiz.q: The potential difference across a capacitor is doubled. Its capacitance
quiz.explain: C depends on geometry and medium only; Q doubles instead.

quiz.q: A parallel plate capacitor's plates have σ = 17.7 × 10⁻⁹ C m⁻². What is the field between them (in V m⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
Why is there a maximum safe voltage rating printed on a capacitor?
options: Above it, the plates melt from current flow
Above it, the field in the dielectric exceeds its dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down
quiz.explain: Breakdown ionises the insulator and lets charge leak across.

quiz.q: Air breaks down at about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. What is the largest voltage that can be applied across an air gap of 1 mm (in kV)?
quiz.mistake: Slips a power of ten in the mm conversion

quiz.q: The field outside an ideal parallel plate capacitor (away from the edges) is
quiz.explain: Fields of the +σ and -σ plates cancel outside.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each plate's field leaks out

quiz.q: A capacitor consists of
options: two insulators separated by a conductor
two conductors separated by an insulator
a coil of wire around an iron core
quiz.explain: The insulator keeps the charges ±Q apart on the two conductors.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a capacitor with an inductor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If I put more charge on a capacitor, does its capacitance increase?'
teach.praise: Chirp! C = Q/V stays the same; it is set by the geometry and the medium. More charge just means more voltage!
teach.nudge: Close! What does capacitance depend on? Does V change when Q changes?

topics.title: Parallel plate capacitor with and without dielectric

learn.hook: How big would a 1 farad parallel plate capacitor with a 1 cm air gap be? Larger than many Indian cities! The farad is a giant unit.
points: Derivation: E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A), V = Ed = Qd/(ε₀A), so C = Q/V = ε₀A/d.
With C = 1 F and d = 1 cm, A = Cd/ε₀ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁹ m², a square about 33 km on each side. Real capacitors are in µF to pF.
With a dielectric filling the gap (charge fixed), the field becomes E₀/K and V becomes V₀/K.
So C = Kε₀A/d = KC₀. Dielectric constant K = ε/ε₀ (relative permittivity) is greater than 1; ε = Kε₀ is the permittivity of the medium. In terms of susceptibility, K = 1 + χe/ε₀.
Typical K values: vacuum 1, air about 1.0006, water about 80, mica about 6, glass 5 to 10.

example.q: A parallel plate capacitor has A = 0.02 m² and d = 1.77 mm, in air. Find C, and C when mica (K = 6) fills the gap. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
example.answer: 100 pF in air; 600 pF with mica

learn.reallife: Touchscreens on phones sold across India work as tiny capacitors: your finger, which is mostly water with high permittivity, changes the local capacitance and the phone senses where you touched.

items.text: Doubling plate area makes C ___.
Doubling the plate separation makes C ___.
Filling with a dielectric of K = 4 makes C ___ times larger.
With charge fixed, a dielectric makes V ___ by K.

quiz.q: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.1 m² separated by 0.885 mm in air. What is its capacitance (in nF)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert mm to m

quiz.q: The gap of a 20 pF air capacitor is completely filled with a dielectric of K = 5. What is the new capacitance (in pF)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by K instead of multiplying

quiz.q: The plate separation of a parallel plate capacitor is tripled and its plate area is doubled. The capacitance becomes
A charged capacitor is disconnected from the battery and a dielectric of K = 4 is inserted. The potential difference becomes
quiz.explain: Q is fixed and C becomes 4C, so V = Q/C becomes V/4.
quiz.mistake: Treats V as fixed when the battery is disconnected

quiz.q: What area (in units of 10⁹ m²) would a 1 F air-filled parallel plate capacitor with a 1 cm gap need? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
quiz.explain: A = Cd/ε₀ = 1 × 0.01/8.85 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 1.13 × 10⁹ m². This shows the farad is a huge unit.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by ε₀ instead of dividing

quiz.q: The dielectric constant K of a medium is defined as
options: the ratio ε/ε₀ of its permittivity to that of free space
the field inside it divided by applied field
quiz.explain: K = ε/ε₀ is dimensionless and greater than 1.

quiz.q: With charge held fixed, inserting a dielectric of constant K into a capacitor makes the field between the plates
quiz.explain: Polarisation reduces the field by a factor K.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the dielectric increases the field

quiz.q: Which material listed would give the largest capacitance when filling the same capacitor?
quiz.explain: Water has K ≈ 80, much larger than mica (≈ 6) and air (≈ 1).
quiz.mistake: Assumes solids always have larger K

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I make my capacitor store more charge at the same voltage?'
teach.praise: Chirp! C = Kε₀A/d: bigger plates, smaller gap, or a dielectric with large K. More charge for the same volts!
teach.nudge: Good! What three things in C = Kε₀A/d could you change?

learn.hook: An Indian electronics hobbyist with only 2 µF capacitors can still make 1 µF, 3 µF or 4 µF. The trick is combining them in series and parallel.
points: Series: each capacitor carries the same charge Q; voltages add. 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + ... (C is less than the smallest).
Parallel: each capacitor has the same voltage V; charges add. C = C₁ + C₂ + ... (C is more than the largest).
Two in series: C = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). n equal capacitors C: series gives C/n, parallel gives nC.
Slab of thickness t (< d) with constant K: C = ε₀A/(d - t + t/K). A metal slab (K → ∞) gives C = ε₀A/(d - t).
To build a required C and voltage rating, put capacitors in series to share the voltage, and parallel rows to increase C.

example.q: A 3 µF and a 6 µF capacitor are in series across 90 V. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge and the voltage on each.
example.answer: C = 2 µF; Q = 180 µC each; 60 V on 3 µF and 30 V on 6 µF

learn.reallife: Power-factor capacitor banks in Indian factories are built by wiring many capacitors in series-parallel groups so that the bank can handle the 11 kV supply and still give the needed capacitance.

learn.hook: Defibrillators in Indian ambulances store around 200 J in a capacitor and dump it into a patient's heart in milliseconds to restore its rhythm.
points: Energy stored: U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV. It is the work done in charging the capacitor.
The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates, with energy density u = ½ε₀E² (per unit volume). With a dielectric, u = ½Kε₀E².

Connecting a charged capacitor to an uncharged one: charge is shared until both reach a common potential V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂). Some energy is always lost as heat and radiation in the connecting wires.
Dielectric inserted with battery connected: V fixed, C → KC, Q → KQ, U → KU.
Dielectric inserted after disconnecting: Q fixed, C → KC, V → V/K, U → U/K.

learn.hook: Electrostatics froze charges in place. Now let them flow, and you get everything from a lightning bolt to the UPI payment pinging on your phone.
points: Moving charges make an electric current. Examples: lightning in a thunderstorm, electrons in battery circuits, ions in electrolytes and in our nerves.
Current I = rate of flow of charge. Steady current: I = q/t. In general I(t) = dq/dt, the limit of Δq/Δt.
SI unit: ampere (A), a base unit; 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹. Smaller units: mA (10⁻³ A) and µA (10⁻⁶ A).
Conventional current is the direction of flow of positive charge, so it is opposite to the flow of electrons.
Typical sizes: household appliances draw a few amperes, nerve signals involve microamperes, while lightning can carry tens of thousands of amperes.

example.q: A charge of 360 C passes through a heater coil in 3 minutes. Find the current.

learn.reallife: Your phone charger's label says, for example, 5 V, 2 A. That 2 A means 2 coulombs of charge flow into the battery every second when charging at full speed.

topics.title: Charge flow in conductors and Ohm's law

learn.hook: Inside a copper wire, electrons zip around at about 10⁶ m s⁻¹, yet without a battery no current flows. Why? Their motion is random.
points: Charge carriers: free electrons in metals; positive and negative ions in electrolytes.
With no field, free electrons move randomly in all directions, so the net flow through any cross-section is zero.
A field applied across the conductor gives electrons a small net drift, producing a current. A cell or other source is needed to keep the field going, or charges would pile up and cancel it.
Ohm's law: for a metallic conductor at constant temperature, V ∝ I, so V = IR. R is the resistance, unit ohm (Ω), 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹.
A graph of V against I for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; its slope is R.

example.q: A 12 V source drives 0.4 A through a resistor. Find R and the current if V is raised to 18 V (same temperature).

learn.reallife: An electrician testing a geyser element in a Pune flat uses a multimeter: measuring V and I and dividing gives R, exactly Ohm's law.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Electrons are already running around in my copper wire. Why do I need a battery?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The electrons move randomly, so there is no net flow. The battery's field gives them a net drift. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good! Is the electrons' motion random or directed, and what does the battery provide?

learn.hook: Why are Indian Railways' overhead lines thick copper alloy, while a geyser element is thin nichrome? It comes down to R = ρl/A.
points: R = ρl/A: resistance is proportional to length l and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A.
Resistivity ρ is a property of the material (and temperature), not of the shape. Unit: Ω m. Copper has ρ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
Conductivity σ = 1/ρ, unit S m⁻¹ (siemens per metre) or Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹.
Current density j = I/A (A m⁻²), and Ohm's law in vector form is j = σE.
Stretching a wire keeps its volume constant: if length becomes n times, area becomes 1/n times, so R becomes n² times.

example.q: A wire of resistance 4 Ω is stretched to twice its length. Find the new resistance.
steps: Volume is constant: l → 2l, A → A/2

learn.reallife: Copper or aluminium is used for transmission lines in India because their low ρ keeps losses down. Nichrome, with high ρ, is chosen for heaters and irons.

topics.title: Drift velocity and the origin of resistance

learn.hook: Electrons in your house wiring crawl at less than a millimetre per second, yet the bulb lights the instant you flip the switch. Both facts are true at once.
points: In a field E, each free electron accelerates (a = -eE/m) between collisions; the average time between collisions is the relaxation time τ.
Drift velocity: vd = -eEτ/m, the average velocity of electrons, opposite to E.
Current I = neAvd, where n is the number density of free electrons and A is the cross-section.
Combining, j = (ne²τ/m)E, so ρ = m/(ne²τ). Resistance arises from collisions.
vd is tiny (about 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹), but the field travels along the wire nearly at the speed of light, so all electrons start drifting almost at once.

example.q: A copper wire (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) of cross-section 10⁻⁶ m² carries 1.36 A. Find vd.

learn.reallife: An Indian Railways signal kilometres away responds instantly when the cabin switch is thrown, even though electrons in the cable barely creep. The field, not the individual electron, carries the signal.

learn.hook: Ohm's law is not a law of nature like gravity; it is a rule many materials obey. Diodes, LEDs and even a hot bulb filament break it.
points: Mobility µ = |vd|/E = eτ/m: drift speed per unit field. SI unit: m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Non-ohmic case 1: the V-I graph is not a straight line, for example a bulb filament whose resistance rises as it heats up at high currents.
Non-ohmic case 2: the relation depends on the sign of V, as in a diode, which conducts much more in one direction.
Non-ohmic case 3: more than one value of V for the same I, as shown by GaAs-type materials.
For non-ohmic devices, V/I is not constant, so a single resistance value does not describe them.

example.q: Electrons drift at 2 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ in a field of 0.04 V m⁻¹. Find their mobility.

learn.reallife: The LED strings used for Diwali lights are non-ohmic devices: they barely conduct until a threshold voltage, and only in one direction.

topics.title: Resistivity of materials and its temperature dependence

learn.hook: From silver to quartz, resistivities span more than 20 orders of magnitude, the biggest range of any common physical property.
points: Materials are classified by resistivity: conductors (metals, about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m), semiconductors (in between) and insulators (up to 10¹⁴ Ω m or more).
The range covers more than 20 orders of magnitude.
For metals, ρ rises with temperature: ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)], where α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (unit K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹).
For metals α is positive. Alloys like manganin and constantan have very small α, so they are used for standard resistors.
Nichrome has high ρ and small α, so it is used in heating elements.

example.q: A wire has R = 20 Ω at 20 °C and α = 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹. Find R at 70 °C.

learn.reallife: Standard resistors at India's National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi are made from alloys like manganin, whose resistance barely changes with room temperature.

quiz.mistake: Thinks standard resistors need very low resistivity

quiz.q: Roughly how many orders of magnitude separate the resistivity of good conductors from that of good insulators?
quiz.explain: From about 10⁻⁸ Ω m for metals to over 10¹⁴ Ω m for insulators: more than 22 orders.

quiz.q: A wire's resistance rises from 10 Ω to 12 Ω when heated by 50 °C. What is α (in units of 10⁻³ °C⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by the final rather than the initial resistance

quiz.q: Going by its resistivity, which of these materials is a semiconductor?
quiz.explain: Silicon's resistivity lies between metals and insulators.

quiz.q: The temperature coefficient of resistivity of a typical metal is
quiz.explain: Resistivity of metals increases with temperature.

quiz.q: In ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)], what does ρ₀ represent?
options: Resistivity at the reference temperature T₀
quiz.explain: It is the value at the reference temperature, often 20 °C or 0 °C.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ρ₀ means resistivity at absolute zero

quiz.q: Why is nichrome preferred for the heating coil of an electric iron?
options: It has high resistivity and its resistance changes little when hot
quiz.explain: High ρ gives large R in a short coil; small α keeps the heating steady.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a heater needs very low resistivity

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a metal wire resist more when it gets hot?'
teach.praise: Chirp! For metals, resistivity rises with temperature: ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)] with positive α. Nice!
teach.nudge: Good! How does the resistivity of a metal depend on temperature?

learn.hook: Heat a copper wire and it resists more. Heat a silicon chip and it conducts better. One formula, ρ = m/(ne²τ), explains both.
points: Semiconductors and insulators: resistivity decreases as temperature rises (negative α).
Using ρ = m/(ne²τ): in metals, n is nearly constant, but hotter ions vibrate more, collisions are more frequent, τ falls, so ρ rises.
In semiconductors, extra heat frees many more charge carriers; the rise in n outweighs the fall in τ, so ρ falls.
Finding the temperature of a heating element: from R and R₀ and α, use T = T₀ + (R - R₀)/(R₀α).
This principle is used in resistance thermometers and in thermistors.

example.q: A heating element has R = 60 Ω at 25 °C (from V/I) and 69 Ω when hot. With α = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹, find the hot temperature.

learn.reallife: Digital thermometers used in Indian clinics often contain a thermistor, a semiconductor whose resistance falls sharply as body heat warms it.

games.title: Metal or semiconductor behaviour?
items: ρ rises with temperature
ρ falls with temperature
n almost constant with temperature
n rises sharply with temperature
Positive α
Negative α

items.text: In metals, heating makes τ ___.
In semiconductors, heating makes n ___.
A thermistor is a ___ device.

quiz.q: Why does the resistivity of a metal increase with temperature?
options: The number of free electrons drops sharply
Collisions become more frequent, so the relaxation time τ decreases
quiz.explain: In ρ = m/(ne²τ), n stays almost constant while τ falls.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of free electrons falls

quiz.q: Why does the resistivity of a semiconductor decrease with temperature?
options: The relaxation time increases a lot
The number density of charge carriers increases rapidly
The mass of the electron decreases
quiz.explain: More bonds break, freeing carriers; this beats the drop in τ.

quiz.q: A heater coil has R = 100 Ω at 20 °C and 120 Ω when hot, with α = 2 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. What is its hot temperature (in °C)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the starting temperature

quiz.q: The temperature coefficient of resistivity of a semiconductor is
options: always equal to that of copper
quiz.explain: Its resistivity falls as temperature rises.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all materials resist more when hot

quiz.q: In the expression ρ = m/(ne²τ), which quantity changes most with temperature in a metal?
quiz.explain: n is fixed by the metal's structure; τ falls as lattice vibrations grow.

quiz.q: A platinum resistance thermometer reads 5 Ω at 0 °C and 6 Ω at an unknown temperature. If α = 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹, what is the temperature (in °C)?
Assertion (A): An insulator's resistivity decreases with increasing temperature. Reason (R): More charge carriers become available as temperature rises. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Like semiconductors, heating frees a few carriers in insulators, lowering resistivity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only metals depend on temperature

quiz.q: Which statement correctly compares heating a copper wire and a silicon crystal?
options: Copper's resistance rises while silicon's falls
quiz.explain: Metals have positive α; semiconductors have negative α.
quiz.mistake: Gives the same trend for both

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Copper resists more when hot, silicon resists less. Who is lying?'
teach.praise: Chirp! In metals τ drops as collisions increase; in semiconductors many more carriers appear. Nobody lies!
teach.nudge: Good! Use ρ = m/(ne²τ). Which factor changes in a metal, and which in a semiconductor?

learn.hook: Your electricity bill counts kilowatt-hours, and every one of them comes from charges falling through potential differences, warming wires on the way.
points: When charge q moves through potential difference V, energy qV is delivered. Power P = VI.
For a resistor, P = VI = I²R = V²/R. This energy appears as heat (Joule heating).
Transmission lines lose power I²Rc in their resistance Rc.
To deliver power P at voltage V, I = P/V, so loss = P²Rc/V². Raising V greatly reduces the loss.
That is why power is sent at very high voltages (hundreds of kV) and stepped down near homes.

example.q: A 1000 W heater runs on 220 V. Find the current and resistance.

learn.reallife: POWERGRID runs 765 kV lines across India so that the current, and hence I²R loss, stays small over thousands of kilometres.

games.title: Power facts
items: Joule heating in a resistor equals I²R per second.
P = I²R.
Sending power at higher voltage increases the current in the line.
For fixed P, higher V means lower I.
The power lost in a line is proportional to the square of the current.
Loss = I²R.
A 100 W bulb has more resistance than a 60 W bulb at the same voltage.
R = V²/P, so the 100 W bulb has less resistance.

quiz.q: A resistor of 10 Ω carries 3 A. What power does it dissipate (in W)?
A 60 W bulb is designed for 240 V. What is its resistance (in Ω)?
A 2 kW geyser runs for 30 minutes a day. How many kWh does it use in 30 days?
quiz.explain: Daily: 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh. In 30 days: 30 kWh.

quiz.q: A power of 100 kW is sent through a line of resistance 0.5 Ω at 10 kV. What is the power lost in the line (in W)?
quiz.mistake: Uses V²/R with the supply voltage, which is not the voltage across the line

quiz.q: If the same 100 kW is sent through the same 0.5 Ω line at 100 kV instead, what is the loss (in W)?
quiz.explain: I = 1 A, loss = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 W, a hundredth of the earlier loss.
quiz.mistake: Thinks loss falls only ten times when V rises ten times

quiz.q: Why is electric power transmitted at very high voltage?
options: Wires have zero resistance at high voltage
For a given power, higher V means lower current and much smaller I²R loss
High voltage is safer for homes
quiz.explain: Loss = P²Rc/V² falls as 1/V².
quiz.mistake: Thinks high voltage itself reduces resistance

quiz.q: Two bulbs of 40 W and 100 W, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
quiz.explain: In series the same current flows, so P = I²R is larger for the larger R. The 40 W bulb has the higher resistance (R = V²/P).
quiz.mistake: Assumes the higher rated bulb always glows brighter

quiz.q: A 5 Ω resistor is connected across 10 V. How much heat is produced in 1 minute (in J)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert 1 minute into 60 s

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why are power lines at lakhs of volts? Isn't that dangerous and wasteful?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Higher voltage means smaller current for the same power, so I²R loss is tiny. Efficient!
teach.nudge: Good! For the same power, how does raising the voltage change the current and the loss?

learn.hook: Why does a car's headlight dim when you crank the starter? The battery's own internal resistance steals voltage when a big current flows.
points: An electrolytic cell has two electrodes in an electrolyte. Its emf ε is the potential difference between its terminals when no current flows.
Every cell has an internal resistance r due to its electrolyte.
With current I drawn through an external resistor R: I = ε/(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε - Ir = IR.
Terminal voltage is less than ε while the cell is delivering current. Maximum current, on short circuit (R = 0), is ε/r.
Emf is not a force; it is energy supplied per unit charge by the cell (unit: volt).

example.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. Find I and V.

learn.reallife: Inverter batteries in Indian homes are rated by emf (12 V) and must have low internal resistance so their voltage does not sag badly when the fridge or fan draws current during a power cut.

items.q: ε = 6 V, r = 1 Ω, R = 5 Ω: I (in A)
Same cell: terminal V (in V)
ε = 1.5 V, r = 0.5 Ω: short-circuit I (in A)
ε = 12 V, I = 2 A, r = 0.5 Ω: V (in V)
Open circuit: terminal V equals

quiz.q: A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 Ω is connected to a 1.2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
A 12 V battery with r = 0.4 Ω supplies 5 A. What is its terminal voltage (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Adds Ir instead of subtracting (that would be charging)

quiz.q: The terminal voltage of a cell is 2.2 V on open circuit and 1.8 V when a current of 2 A flows. What is the internal resistance (in Ω)?
quiz.mistake: Divides the terminal voltage by the current

quiz.q: What is the maximum current that can be drawn from a cell of emf 9 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω (in A)?
quiz.explain: Short circuit: I = ε/r = 9/0.5 = 18 A.

quiz.q: Why is the terminal voltage of a cell less than its emf when it supplies current?
options: Charge is lost inside the cell
Part of the emf is used to drive current through the internal resistance (Ir drop)
The external resistor increases the emf
quiz.explain: V = ε - Ir.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the emf itself drops instantly

quiz.q: Emf of a cell is best described as
options: the internal resistance of the cell
the energy supplied per unit charge by the cell, equal to the terminal p.d. on open circuit
quiz.explain: Despite its name, emf is not a force; it is measured in volts.

quiz.q: A cell gives 0.5 A through a 4 Ω resistor and 0.25 A through a 9 Ω resistor. What is its emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores internal resistance and uses V = IR for one case only

quiz.q: A cell with ε = 2 V, r = 1 Ω is connected to R = 1 Ω. What is the power delivered to R (in W)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the internal resistance when finding I

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My 1.5 V cell shows only 1.3 V across the bulb. Is the cell lying?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Some voltage, Ir, is used up inside the cell, so terminal voltage = ε - Ir. Honest cell!
teach.nudge: Good! What is inside a cell that uses up part of its emf when current flows?

topics.title: Cells in series and in parallel

learn.hook: A torch uses cells in series for more voltage. Solar panel farms in Rajasthan combine panels in series and parallel to get both voltage and current.
points: Two cells in series (positive of one to negative of the other): ε_eq = ε₁ + ε₂ and r_eq = r₁ + r₂. If one cell is reversed, ε_eq = ε₁ - ε₂ while r_eq still adds.
Two cells in parallel: ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂.
n identical cells (ε, r) in series: emf nε, resistance nr. m identical cells in parallel: emf ε, resistance r/m.
Mixed grouping (m parallel rows, each of n cells in series): ε_eq = nε and r_eq = nr/m; current I = nε/(R + nr/m).
Series increases voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance and lets more current be drawn.

example.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 1 V with internal resistances 1 Ω and 2 Ω are joined in parallel. Find ε_eq and r_eq.

learn.reallife: Electric rickshaws on Indian streets typically use four 12 V batteries in series, giving 48 V to drive the motor.

items.q: 4 cells of 1.5 V in series: emf (in V)
4 cells of 1.5 V in parallel: emf (in V)
3 cells, r = 0.6 Ω each, in series: r_eq (in Ω)
3 cells, r = 0.6 Ω each, in parallel: r_eq (in Ω)
Cells of 6 V and 4 V in series, one reversed: emf (in V)

games.title: Grouping rules
items: In series, the internal resistances add.
r_eq = r₁ + r₂.
Reversing one cell in a series pair also subtracts its internal resistance.
Emfs subtract but resistances still add.
Identical cells in parallel have the same emf as a single cell.
ε_eq = ε for identical cells.
Parallel grouping increases the internal resistance.
It decreases it to r/m.
Two parallel cells with ε₁ ≠ ε₂ have an emf between ε₁ and ε₂.
ε_eq is a weighted average.

quiz.q: Two cells of 1.5 V (r = 0.5 Ω each) are in series with a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
Cells of emf 6 V (r = 1 Ω) and 2 V (r = 1 Ω) are connected in series with opposite polarity across a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the emfs despite reversed polarity

quiz.q: Two cells of 4 V and 2 V with internal resistances 2 Ω and 2 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Adds the emfs as in series

quiz.q: Six identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.6 Ω, are arranged as 2 parallel rows of 3 cells in series. What is the internal resistance of the combination (in Ω)?
quiz.mistake: Uses n × r without dividing by the number of rows

quiz.q: For the same arrangement (2 rows of 3 cells of 2 V, 0.6 Ω each) connected to a 5.1 Ω resistor, what is the current (in A)?
quiz.mistake: Takes emf as 12 V by adding all six cells

quiz.q: Four identical cells (ε, r) are connected in parallel. The equivalent emf and internal resistance are
quiz.explain: Identical cells in parallel keep emf ε and divide r by the number of cells.
quiz.mistake: Uses the series rule for emf

quiz.q: Why are cells connected in parallel when a large current is needed at low voltage?
options: Parallel grouping reduces the internal resistance, so more current can flow
It makes the cells last a shorter time
quiz.explain: r_eq = r/m drops, raising the maximum current.

quiz.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 2 V with internal resistances 1 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel. What is the equivalent internal resistance (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂) = 3/4 = 0.75 Ω.

teach.ask: Gappu has many cells and asks: 'How do I get more voltage? And how do I get more current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Series adds the emfs for more voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance for more current. Power up!
teach.nudge: Good! Which grouping adds the emfs, and which reduces the internal resistance?

learn.hook: Some circuits cannot be reduced to simple series and parallel parts. Gustav Kirchhoff gave two rules that crack any network, from a torch to the national grid.
points: Junction rule: at any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving. This is conservation of charge.
Loop rule: the algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop is zero. This is conservation of energy.
Sign convention: going across a resistor in the direction of the assumed current, the potential drops (-IR); against it, it rises (+IR). Going from - to + terminal of a cell, potential rises (+ε).
If a current comes out negative, it simply flows opposite to the direction assumed.
Symmetry helps: in a cube of 12 equal resistors R, the resistance between opposite corners is 5R/6.

example.q: At a junction, 3 A and 2 A flow in along two wires, and 1.5 A flows out along a third. What flows in the fourth wire?
steps: Sum out must also be 5 A
example.answer: 3.5 A flowing out of the junction

learn.reallife: Power engineers at India's National Load Despatch Centre use network equations based on Kirchhoff's rules to balance power flows between regional grids every minute.

games.title: Rule and principle
pairs: Current flows opposite to the assumed direction

games.title: Solving a network
items: Mark an assumed current in each branch
Apply the junction rule at junctions
Choose independent closed loops
Apply the loop rule with sign conventions
Solve the equations and interpret signs

quiz.q: At a junction, currents of 4 A and 3 A enter and a current of 5 A leaves along one wire. What current leaves through the only other wire (in A)?
quiz.explain: In = out: 4 + 3 = 5 + I, so I = 2 A.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is a consequence of
quiz.explain: A charge that goes round a loop returns to the same potential, so no net energy is gained or lost.

quiz.q: In a loop, you go across a 4 Ω resistor in the direction opposite to its current of 2 A. The change in potential is (in V)
quiz.explain: Going against the current, potential rises by IR = +8 V.

quiz.q: A single loop has a 10 V cell (negligible r) and resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series. Using the loop rule, what is the current (in A)?
A loop contains a 12 V cell and a 4 V cell connected to oppose each other, with a total resistance of 4 Ω (including internal resistances). What is the current (in A)?
quiz.explain: Net emf = 12 - 4 = 8 V. I = 8/4 = 2 A, in the direction driven by the 12 V cell.

quiz.q: While solving a network, a current comes out as -0.5 A. This means
options: the current is 0.5 A but flows opposite to the direction assumed
quiz.explain: The assumed direction was just a guess; the sign corrects it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative current is impossible

quiz.q: Twelve equal resistors of 6 Ω form the edges of a cube. What is the equivalent resistance between two diagonally opposite corners (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: R_eq = 5R/6 = 5 × 6/6 = 5 Ω (by symmetry: current I splits into 3, then 6, then 3 parts).
steps: By symmetry I splits into I/3, then I/6, then I/3
quiz.mistake: Forgets the symmetric splitting of current

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on
quiz.explain: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in steady state.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are the two Kirchhoff rules, and why are they true?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Junction rule: current in = out (charge conservation). Loop rule: potential changes add to zero (energy conservation). Woohoo!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each rule say, and which conservation law is behind it?

learn.hook: Before digital meters, the Wheatstone bridge was the gold standard for measuring resistance. It still hides inside weighing scales and strain gauges.
points: Four resistors P, Q, R and S form a diamond ABCD: P from A to B, Q from B to C, R from A to D, S from D to C. A cell is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer across B and D.
Balanced bridge: no current flows through the galvanometer, so B and D are at the same potential.
Applying Kirchhoff's rules with Ig = 0 gives the balance condition P/Q = R/S.
If three resistances are known, the fourth is found from the balance condition: S = RQ/P.
If the bridge is not balanced, a current flows through the galvanometer; it is found using Kirchhoff's rules.

example.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, P = 100 Ω, Q = 10 Ω and R = 30 Ω. Find the unknown S.

learn.reallife: Digital weighing scales at Indian kirana shops use strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge: the weight slightly changes one arm's resistance, unbalancing the bridge in proportion to the load.

items.text: At balance, the current through the galvanometer is ___.
Balance condition: P/Q = R/___.
At balance, points B and D are at the same ___.
A bridge with Ig ≠ 0 is called ___.

items.q: P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 3 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 10 Ω, Q = 10 Ω, R = 7 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 5 Ω, Q = 1 Ω, R = 20 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 100 Ω, Q = 50 Ω, R = 40 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 3 Ω, Q = 9 Ω, R = 2 Ω: S (in Ω)

quiz.q: A Wheatstone bridge balances with P = 8 Ω, Q = 2 Ω and R = 12 Ω. What is S (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: P/Q = R/S gives S = RQ/P = 24/8 = 3 Ω.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio and gets 48 Ω

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge, why does no current flow through the galvanometer?
options: The two ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential
The currents in all four arms are equal
quiz.explain: Current flows only if there is a potential difference across the galvanometer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks balance needs all arms to carry equal current

quiz.q: Four resistors P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 6 Ω and S = 12 Ω form a bridge. Is it balanced?
options: No, since P + Q ≠ R + S
Only if the cell emf is 6 V
quiz.explain: 2/4 = 6/12 = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced whatever the cell.

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge, the galvanometer and the cell are interchanged. The bridge
quiz.explain: The condition P/Q = R/S is symmetric; swapping cell and galvanometer keeps balance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks positions of cell and galvanometer matter for balance

quiz.q: A bridge has P = Q = R = 10 Ω and S = 10 Ω with a galvanometer of 20 Ω. If S is changed to 20 Ω, will a galvanometer current flow?
options: No, because the galvanometer resistance is large
Only if the cell is reversed
quiz.explain: Balance needs P/Q = R/S; now 1 ≠ 1/2, so the bridge is unbalanced.
quiz.mistake: Thinks P = Q alone ensures balance

quiz.q: In bridge ABCD, P = 1 Ω (A to B), Q = 2 Ω (B to C), R = 2 Ω (A to D) and S = 1 Ω (D to C). A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer of resistance 2 Ω across B and D. What current flows through the galvanometer (in A)?
quiz.explain: P/Q = 1/2 but R/S = 2, so the bridge is unbalanced. Taking V_C = 0 and V_A = 10 V, the junction rule at B and D gives V_B = 6 V and V_D = 4 V, so Ig = (6 - 4)/2 = 1 A, from B to D.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the galvanometer current is zero without checking the balance condition

quiz.q: When a bridge is balanced, the galvanometer can be removed without changing any current. Why?
options: Because it is in series with the cell
It carries zero current, so removing it changes nothing
quiz.explain: A branch with zero current can be removed (or replaced by any resistor) without effect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every branch affects the network

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 6 Ω and S = 9 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?
A wire of resistance 8 Ω is used as S in a balanced bridge with P = 2 Ω and Q = 4 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is so special about a balanced Wheatstone bridge?'
teach.praise: Chirp! At balance the galvanometer shows zero current because its ends are at the same potential, and P/Q = R/S. Bridge mastered!
teach.nudge: Good! What does the galvanometer show at balance, and what condition holds?

learn.hook: In 1820, during a lecture demonstration, Hans Christian Oersted saw a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire. Electricity and magnetism were joined for good.
points: Oersted's discovery (1820): a current in a straight wire deflects a nearby compass needle. The needle sets along circles around the wire.
Moving charges (currents) produce magnetic fields. Reversing the current reverses the deflection.
Later, Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism and showed light is an electromagnetic wave.
Notation: a dot ⊙ means a field or current coming out of the page (towards you); a cross ⊗ means going into the page.
Magnetic fields obey superposition: the field of several sources is the vector sum of their individual fields. Like E, B is a vector field.

example.q: A compass is placed just below a wire running north-south. When the current flows north, the needle's north pole swings west. What happens if the current is reversed?
steps: Below a wire carrying current northwards, the field points west (right-hand thumb rule), so the north pole swings west.
Reversing the current reverses the field around the wire.
The force on the needle's poles reverses, so it swings the other way.
example.answer: The north pole now swings east

learn.reallife: Railway engineers keep sensitive magnetic compasses and instruments away from heavy-current traction cables on electrified Indian Railways routes, because the current's magnetic field can deflect them.

games.title: Oersted's lessons
items: A steady current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it.
That was Oersted's observation.
A stationary charge produces a magnetic field.
Only moving charges (currents) do.
The symbol ⊗ means a field directed into the page.
Think of the tail feathers of an arrow going away.
Magnetic fields from two sources add as vectors.
Superposition holds for B.
Reversing the current leaves the compass deflection unchanged.
The deflection reverses.

quiz.q: Who first observed that an electric current deflects a magnetic compass needle?
quiz.explain: Oersted noticed this in 1820, linking electricity and magnetism.
quiz.mistake: Credits Faraday, who later discovered induction

quiz.q: In a diagram, a magnetic field pointing straight towards the reader is shown by
quiz.explain: A dot is like the tip of an arrow coming at you.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the dot and cross conventions

quiz.q: A compass placed near a straight wire with current tends to align
options: along circles centred on the wire
quiz.explain: The field of a straight wire forms concentric circles around it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field is along the wire

quiz.q: Which of these produces a magnetic field?
options: A charged comb kept on a table
A neutral atom at rest with no magnetic moment
quiz.explain: Moving charges make magnetic fields; static charges make only electric fields.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any charge makes a magnetic field

quiz.q: Two wires each produce a field of 3 µT at a point, in the same direction. What is the net field there (in µT)?
quiz.explain: Superposition: same direction, so the fields add: 3 + 3 = 6 µT.

quiz.q: Two wires produce fields of 3 µT (east) and 4 µT (north) at a point. What is the magnitude of the net field (in µT)?
quiz.explain: Fields add as vectors: √(3² + 4²) = 5 µT.

quiz.q: Maxwell's work showed that
options: electricity and magnetism are unified, and light is an electromagnetic wave
currents do not produce magnetic fields
light is a stream of electrons
quiz.explain: Maxwell's equations predicted EM waves moving at the speed of light.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A compass needle deflects near a wire only while current flows. Reason (R): Only moving charges produce magnetic fields. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: When the current stops, the charges no longer drift, so there is no magnetic field to turn the needle.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the field to the motion of charges

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does my compass go crazy near a wire with current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Moving charges in the wire make a magnetic field around it, which turns the compass. Thanks, Oersted!
teach.nudge: Good! What does a current produce around it?

topics.title: Lorentz force on a moving charge

learn.hook: Charged particles from the Sun are steered by Earth's magnetic field into the polar skies, painting the auroras. The steering force is the Lorentz force.
points: Lorentz force: F = q[E + v × B]. The magnetic part is F = q(v × B), magnitude qvB sinθ.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to both v and B. It is zero if the charge is at rest or moves along B (θ = 0 or 180°).
Direction: use the right-hand rule for v × B (fingers along v, curl towards B, thumb gives the force on a positive charge). Reverse it for a negative charge.
SI unit of B: tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹. Smaller unit: gauss, 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T.
Typical fields: Earth's surface about 10⁻⁵ T; a lab magnet about 1 T; a neutron star about 10⁸ T.

example.q: A proton moves at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. Find the force on it.
example.answer: 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N, perpendicular to both v and B

learn.reallife: Auroras are rarely seen from India, but ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory studies the solar wind whose charged particles feel the Lorentz force as they reach Earth's magnetic field.

games.title: Lorentz force check
items: The magnetic force on a charge at rest is zero.
v = 0 means qv × B = 0.
A charge moving parallel to B feels the maximum magnetic force.
sin 0° = 0, so the force is zero.
The magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity.
It comes from a cross product with v.
1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ tesla.
So Earth's ~0.5 G field is ~5 × 10⁻⁵ T.
An electron and a proton moving the same way in the same field feel forces in the same direction.
Opposite charges get opposite forces.

quiz.q: An electron moves at 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a field of 0.2 T. What is the magnitude of the force on it (in units of 10⁻¹⁴ N)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: A charge of 2 µC moves at 10⁴ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a field of 0.5 T. What is the magnetic force (in mN)?
A proton moves along +x in a field along +y. What is the direction of the magnetic force on it?
quiz.explain: F = q(v × B) = e(x̂ × ŷ) = +eẑ.
quiz.mistake: Uses the left-hand order or forgets the cross product

quiz.q: An electron moves along +x in a field along +y. The magnetic force on it points along
quiz.explain: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, and the negative charge flips it to -z.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reverse the direction for a negative charge

quiz.q: A charged particle moves through a region with no deflection. Which conclusion is certain?
options: It cannot be concluded that B = 0, since the particle may be moving along B
The particle must be at rest
quiz.explain: A charge moving parallel to B feels no magnetic force, so the field could be non-zero.
quiz.mistake: Assumes no deflection always means no field

quiz.q: Why does the magnetic force not change the speed of a charge?
options: It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
It acts only on charges at rest
It is parallel to the velocity
quiz.explain: A force perpendicular to motion changes direction but not kinetic energy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any force must change the speed

quiz.q: Which is the SI unit of magnetic field?
quiz.explain: The tesla (T) is the SI unit; the gauss is a smaller non-SI unit.

quiz.q: The Lorentz force on a charge q in combined fields is
quiz.explain: Electric force qE plus magnetic force q(v × B).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which field the velocity multiplies

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a magnetic field pushes a moving charge, why doesn't the charge speed up?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. It only turns the charge!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the angle between the magnetic force and the velocity?

learn.hook: Every electric motor, from a ceiling fan to an electric scooter, works because a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field gets a push.
points: A straight conductor of length l carrying current I in a uniform field B feels F = I l × B, magnitude BIl sinθ.
This is just the sum of Lorentz forces on the drifting electrons in the wire.
Direction: l points along the current; use the right-hand rule (or Fleming's left-hand rule).
A horizontal wire can float if the magnetic force balances its weight: BIl = mg.
On individual charges, the magnetic force does no work, so their speed stays constant.

example.q: A 0.2 m wire of mass 20 g lies horizontally in a horizontal field of 0.5 T perpendicular to it. What current makes it float? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)

learn.reallife: Loudspeakers in a Bollywood cinema hall use a coil in a magnet's field. The force BIl on the coil changes with the audio current and moves the speaker cone.

items.q: Wire parallel to B: F (in N)

The force on a wire is along the direction of the current.

F ∝ I.

It does no work on them.

quiz.q: A wire 0.5 m long carries 4 A at right angles to a field of 0.3 T. What force acts on it (in N)?
A 10 cm wire carries 5 A at 30° to a 0.8 T field. What is the force on it (in N)?
