A horizontal wire carries current towards the north in a magnetic field pointing vertically upward. In which direction is the force on the wire?
quiz.explain: F = I l × B. Taking x = east, y = north and z = up: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so the force points east.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of the cross product and gets west

quiz.q: Why does a magnetic field do no work on the charges in a wire, even though the wire itself can be pushed?
options: Work is done only on protons
The force on each charge is perpendicular to its velocity
quiz.explain: Each charge's magnetic force is perpendicular to its motion, so no work is done on it directly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the magnetic field directly supplies the energy

quiz.q: The force on a straight conductor in a uniform field is given by
quiz.explain: F = I l × B, with l along the current.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the cross product or uses a dot product

quiz.q: The current in a wire is doubled and the field is halved. The force on the wire
Assertion (A): A current-carrying wire placed along a magnetic field feels no force. Reason (R): The force on a wire is BIl sinθ, and θ = 0 here. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin 0° = 0, so the force vanishes when the wire is parallel to B.
quiz.mistake: Does not apply the sinθ factor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a motor get its push from a magnet?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels F = BIl sinθ, which pushes the coil round. Vroom!
teach.nudge: Good! What force acts on a wire carrying current in a magnetic field?

topics.title: Circular and helical motion in a magnetic field

learn.hook: Particle accelerators and mass spectrometers bend charged particles into circles with magnets. The radius tells you the particle's momentum.
points: A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B moves in a circle: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB) = p/(qB).
Angular frequency ω = qB/m; frequency ν = qB/(2πm); period T = 2πm/(qB). These do not depend on speed or radius (cyclotron frequency).
If v has a component v∥ along B, that part is unaffected, while v⊥ makes the circle: the path is a helix.
Pitch of the helix = distance moved along B in one revolution = v∥T = 2πm v∥/(qB). Radius r = mv⊥/(qB).
Faster particles make bigger circles but take the same time per revolution.

example.q: An electron moves at 4 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 9.1 × 10⁻⁴ T. Find the radius of its path. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

learn.reallife: Mass spectrometers at BARC, Mumbai, separate isotopes by bending ions in a magnetic field: heavier ions of the same charge and speed curve along larger radii.

games.title: Circling charges
items: The period of a charge circling in a uniform B depends on its speed.
T = 2πm/(qB) has no v.
Doubling the speed doubles the radius.
r ∝ v.
A charge entering at an angle to B follows a helix.
v∥ is unchanged while v⊥ circles.
The kinetic energy of the circling charge increases each revolution.
Magnetic force does no work.
A heavier ion with the same charge and speed moves on a larger circle.
r ∝ m.

quiz.q: A proton (m = 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.1 T. What is the radius of its circular path (in cm)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: The speed of a charged particle moving in a circle in a uniform magnetic field is doubled. Its period of revolution
quiz.explain: T = 2πm/(qB) is independent of speed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a faster particle must finish the circle sooner

quiz.q: A charged particle moving in a circle in a field B has radius 4 cm. If B is doubled (same speed), the radius becomes (in cm)
quiz.explain: r = mv/(qB) ∝ 1/B, so r halves.

quiz.q: A particle with v∥ = 3 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ along B has a period of 2 × 10⁻⁶ s for its circular part. What is the pitch of its helix (in m)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the perpendicular component instead of the parallel one

quiz.q: Which expression gives the angular frequency of a charge in a uniform magnetic field?
quiz.explain: From qvB = mω²r and v = ωr: ω = qB/m.

quiz.q: An alpha particle (charge 2e, mass 4m) and a proton (charge e, mass m) enter the same field with the same speed, perpendicular to B. What is r(alpha)/r(proton)?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the charge of the alpha particle

quiz.q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at 60° to B. Its path will be
options: a helix with its axis along B
a circle in a plane containing B
quiz.explain: The component along B is unchanged; the perpendicular component gives circular motion. Together, a helix.

quiz.q: An electron and a proton enter a uniform field perpendicularly with the same momentum. Which statement is correct?
options: The electron's circle is much bigger
The proton's circle is much bigger
They move on circles of the same radius but in opposite senses
quiz.explain: r = p/(qB) is the same for equal p and |q|, but opposite charges curve in opposite directions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the lighter particle always curves more

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a charge goes faster in a magnetic field, does it go round quicker?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Faster means a bigger circle, but the period 2πm/(qB) stays the same. Tricky!
teach.nudge: Good! How do the radius and the period depend on speed?

learn.hook: Coulomb's law gives the field of a point charge. For magnetism there are no magnetic charges, so Biot and Savart built the field from tiny pieces of current instead.
points: Biot-Savart law: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r/r³, magnitude dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r², where θ is between dl and r.
µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ (permeability of free space), so µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
Similarities with Coulomb's law: both are inverse-square and long-range, and both obey superposition.
Differences: the source is a vector (I dl) not a scalar charge; dB depends on the angle θ and is perpendicular to both dl and r; dB = 0 along the line of the element.
Remarkably, µ₀ε₀ = 1/c², so c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

example.q: An element dl = 1 cm carrying 10 A lies along x. Find dB at 0.5 m along y from it.

learn.reallife: Engineers designing MRI machines for Indian hospitals compute the field of every turn of the coils by adding Biot-Savart contributions from tiny current elements.

games.title: Coulomb, Biot-Savart or both?
items: Inverse-square dependence
Source is a scalar charge
Source is a vector element I dl
Field depends on angle sinθ
Superposition holds
Field along the line joining source and point

items.text: dB is zero along the ___ of the current element.
dB depends on I dl sinθ divided by ___.

quiz.q: A current element of 2 A and length 5 mm is perpendicular to the line joining it to a point 10 cm away. What is dB at that point (in µT)?
For the same element (2 A, 5 mm), what is dB at a point 10 cm away along the line of the element (in µT)?
quiz.explain: θ = 0 along the element, and sin 0 = 0.

quiz.q: What is the value of µ₀/4π in SI units?
quiz.explain: µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷, so dividing by 4π leaves 10⁻⁷.
quiz.mistake: Gives µ₀ itself or the electrostatic constant

quiz.q: In the Biot-Savart law, the direction of dB is
options: perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r
quiz.explain: dB ∝ dl × r, so it is perpendicular to both.
quiz.mistake: Thinks B points along r as E does

quiz.q: Which is a key difference between the Biot-Savart law and Coulomb's law?
options: The magnetic field depends on the angle between the current element and the position vector
Only the Biot-Savart law obeys superposition
Coulomb's law depends on a vector source
quiz.explain: The sinθ factor and the vector source I dl are unique to Biot-Savart.

quiz.q: Using µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the value of 1/√(µ₀ε₀) is close to
quiz.explain: 1/√(µ₀ε₀) = c, the speed of light.

quiz.q: A current element at the origin points along +x. What is the direction of dB at a point on the +y axis?
quiz.explain: dl × r = x̂ × ŷ = ẑ.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of the cross product

quiz.q: A current element produces dB at a distance r. What is dB at 2r in the same direction (θ unchanged)?
quiz.explain: dB ∝ 1/r².

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a tiny bit of current wire make a magnetic field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! By the Biot-Savart law, dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r². Add all the bits to get the full field!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law gives the field of a small current element, and how does it depend on angle and distance?

topics.title: Field of a circular current loop

learn.hook: Coil a wire into a loop and the field at its centre gets concentrated. Wind many loops and you have the coils of motors, speakers and MRI scanners.
points: On the axis of a loop of radius R at distance x from the centre: B = µ₀IR²/[2(x² + R²)^(3/2)], along the axis (from Biot-Savart; the perpendicular parts cancel by symmetry).
At the centre (x = 0): B = µ₀I/(2R). For N turns: B = µ₀NI/(2R).
For an arc subtending angle θ (in radians) at its centre: B = µ₀Iθ/(4πR). A semicircle gives µ₀I/(4R).
Right-hand thumb rule for a loop: curl the fingers along the current, and the thumb points along B through the loop.
Field lines of a loop are like those of a short bar magnet: they come out of one face and go into the other.

example.q: A coil of 200 turns, radius 8 cm, carries 0.5 A. Find B at its centre. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: The tangent galvanometer, once common in Indian college labs, uses the field at the centre of a circular coil, µ₀NI/2R, balanced against Earth's horizontal field.

games.title: Loop logic
items: At the centre of a loop, the field is perpendicular to the plane of the loop.
It is along the axis.
The field on the axis of a loop increases as you move away from the centre.
It is largest at the centre and falls with x.
Viewed from one side, a counter-clockwise current produces a field pointing towards the viewer.
Right-hand thumb rule.
Doubling the radius of a loop (same current) doubles the field at its centre.
B ∝ 1/R, so it halves.
A current loop's field lines resemble those of a bar magnet.
A loop is a magnetic dipole.

quiz.q: A single circular loop of radius 6.28 cm carries 10 A. What is the field at its centre (in µT)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 in the denominator

quiz.q: A coil of 50 turns and radius 3.14 cm carries 2 A. What is B at its centre (in mT)? (π = 3.14)
A semicircular wire of radius 5 cm carries 4 A. What is the field at its centre (in µT)? (π = 3.14)
The field at the centre of a loop is B. The same wire is bent into a loop of half the radius with 2 turns, carrying the same current. The new field at the centre is
quiz.explain: N doubles and R halves: B ∝ N/R gives 2/(1/2) = 4.
quiz.mistake: Considers only one of the two changes

quiz.q: On the axis of a loop of radius R, at a distance x = R from the centre, the field compared with the centre value B₀ is
quiz.mistake: Uses the inverse-square law along the axis

quiz.q: Why do the field components perpendicular to the axis cancel for a circular loop?
options: Elements on opposite ends of a diameter give equal and opposite perpendicular components
The field is zero everywhere off the axis
The current is zero in half the loop
Only the axial component exists for any wire
quiz.explain: By symmetry, the perpendicular components from diametrically opposite elements cancel in pairs.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the symmetry argument

quiz.q: A loop lies in the plane of the page with current flowing clockwise as you look at it. The field at its centre points
quiz.explain: Curl right-hand fingers clockwise: the thumb points into the page.

quiz.q: A quarter-circle arc of radius R carries current I. What is B at its centre?
quiz.explain: θ = π/2: B = µ₀I(π/2)/(4πR) = µ₀I/(8R).

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the direction of the magnetic field inside a current loop?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Curl the right-hand fingers along the current and the thumb points along B through the loop. Easy!
teach.nudge: Good! Which hand rule do we use, and what do the fingers and thumb represent?

topics.title: Ampere's circuital law and the straight wire

learn.hook: Gauss's law makes symmetric electric problems easy. Ampere's law does the same for magnetic fields of straight wires, cylinders and solenoids.
points: Ampere's circuital law: ∮B·dl = µ₀I, where I is the net current passing through the closed loop (the Amperian loop).
Choose a loop where B is constant and tangent (or normal, so B·dl = 0) by symmetry, just as a Gaussian surface is chosen for Gauss's law.
Long straight wire: a circle of radius r gives B(2πr) = µ₀I, so B = µ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ I/r.
Direction: right-hand thumb rule. Thumb along the current, curled fingers give the circular field lines.
Long solid cylinder of radius a with uniform current I: outside B = µ₀I/(2πr); inside B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²), rising linearly from zero at the axis.

example.q: A long straight wire carries 5 A. Find B at 10 cm.
example.answer: 1 × 10⁻⁵ T, in circles around the wire

learn.reallife: Near a 765 kV transmission line carrying about 1000 A, the field 20 m below is about 10 µT, roughly a fifth of Earth's field. This is what B = µ₀I/(2πr) predicts.

games.title: Ampere's law for a straight wire

Choose a circular Amperian loop of radius r
B is constant and tangent along the loop
∮B·dl = B × 2πr
Set equal to µ₀I and solve: B = µ₀I/(2πr)

∮B·dl = µ₀I_enc.
The field of a long straight wire falls as 1/r².
It falls as 1/r.
Inside a long uniform cylindrical conductor, B increases linearly with distance from the axis.
B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²).
Currents outside the Amperian loop contribute to the enclosed current.
Only currents through the loop count.
The field at the axis of a long cylindrical conductor is zero.
No current is enclosed at r = 0.

quiz.q: A long straight wire carries 10 A. What is the magnetic field 5 cm from it (in µT)?
The field 2 cm from a long wire is 60 µT. What is the field 6 cm from it (in µT)?
quiz.explain: B ∝ 1/r, so tripling r gives 60/3 = 20 µT.

quiz.q: A long wire carries current vertically upward. Viewed from above, the field lines around it are
quiz.explain: Point the right thumb up: fingers curl counter-clockwise as seen from above.
quiz.mistake: Applies the rule with the left hand

quiz.q: A long solid cylinder of radius 2 cm carries 4 A uniformly. What is B at 1 cm from the axis (in µT)?
For the same cylinder (4 A, radius 2 cm), what is B at 4 cm from the axis (in µT)?
Ampere's circuital law states that ∮B·dl equals
options: µ₀ times the total current anywhere
µ₀ times the net current through the loop
quiz.explain: Only current crossing the surface bounded by the loop counts.

quiz.q: Two long wires pass through a closed loop: one carries 3 A upward and the other 5 A downward. A third wire, outside the loop, carries 10 A upward. Taking upward as positive, what is ∮B·dl in units of µ₀ (in A)?
quiz.explain: Only enclosed currents: 3 - 5 = -2 A, so ∮B·dl = -2µ₀.

quiz.q: Ampere's law plays the same role for magnetic fields that which law plays for electric fields?
quiz.explain: Both use symmetry with a chosen surface or loop to find fields simply.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I find the magnetic field of a long wire without adding up every tiny bit?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Use Ampere's law with a circular loop: B × 2πr = µ₀I, so B = µ₀I/2πr. Symmetry saves the day!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law and which shape of loop make this easy?

learn.hook: Wind a wire tightly into a long coil and you can create a strong, uniform magnetic field inside, a magnet you can switch on and off.
points: A long solenoid has a nearly uniform field inside along its axis, and a nearly zero field outside.
Ampere's law with a rectangular loop (one side inside, one outside) gives BL = µ₀(nL)I, so B = µ₀nI, where n = N/L is turns per unit length.
B inside does not depend on the radius or the exact position inside (for a long solenoid).
The solenoid's field resembles a bar magnet's: one end acts as a north pole, the other as a south pole. Use the right-hand rule to find which end is north.
At each end of a long solenoid the field is about half the value inside, µ₀nI/2.

example.q: A solenoid 0.4 m long has 600 turns and carries 2 A. Find B inside. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: Electric doorbells and the solenoid valves in Indian washing machines use solenoids: switching on the current magnetises the coil and pulls an iron plunger.

items.text: B inside a long solenoid = µ₀___I, with turns per metre n.
Field outside a long solenoid is nearly ___.
Doubling turns per metre ___ B.
A solenoid's field looks like that of a ___ magnet.

items.q: n = 1000 m⁻¹, I = 1 A: B (in mT)
n = 2000 m⁻¹, I = 5 A: B (in mT)
100 turns in 10 cm: n (per m)
Same solenoid, current doubled: B becomes
Same solenoid, radius doubled: B becomes

quiz.q: A solenoid has 2000 turns per metre and carries 2.5 A. What is the field inside (in mT)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, π = 3.14)
A solenoid is 40 cm long with 800 turns and carries 0.5 A. What is the field inside (in mT)? (π = 3.14)
quiz.mistake: Uses the total number of turns instead of n

quiz.q: The number of turns of a solenoid is doubled while its length and current are kept the same. The field inside
quiz.explain: B = µ₀(N/L)I ∝ N.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more turns spread the field out

quiz.q: Why do we take the field outside a long solenoid as zero in the Ampere's law derivation?
options: The outside is shielded by the wire
The field lines outside are spread over a very large region, so the field there is negligible
The field outside is equal and opposite to that inside
quiz.explain: The return field spreads out widely and is very weak compared with the concentrated field inside.
quiz.mistake: Thinks there is absolutely no field outside any solenoid

quiz.q: In the Ampere's law derivation for a solenoid, the rectangular loop has length L inside. The enclosed current is
quiz.explain: nL turns pass through the loop, each carrying I.

quiz.q: A long solenoid produces 2 mT inside. What is the field near either end on the axis (in mT)?
quiz.explain: At the ends of a long solenoid the field is about half the inside value.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field is the same at the ends

quiz.q: A solenoid's field inside depends on
options: turns per unit length and current
quiz.explain: B = µ₀nI.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a thicker solenoid has a weaker field

quiz.q: Looking at one end of a solenoid, the current flows counter-clockwise. That end behaves as a
quiz.explain: Right-hand rule: fingers counter-clockwise, thumb towards you, so field lines come out of that end: north pole.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I make a strong magnetic field I can switch on and off?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Wind a solenoid: B = µ₀nI, so more turns per metre or more current makes it stronger. Switchable magnet!
teach.nudge: Good! Which device does this, and what does its field depend on?

learn.hook: Two parallel wires both carrying current towards the same end pull towards each other. That tiny tug was once the official definition of the ampere.
points: Wire a creates B = µ₀Ia/(2πd) at wire b. Force per unit length on b: f = µ₀IaIb/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ IaIb/d.
Currents in the same direction (parallel) attract; currents in opposite directions (antiparallel) repel. This is opposite to the rule for like charges.
The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite (Newton's third law).
Historical definition (used until 2019): one ampere is the current which, in two long straight parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length.
Since 2019, the ampere is defined by fixing the value of the elementary charge e.

example.q: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 8 A in the same direction. Find the force per metre.

learn.reallife: In large power stations and substations, bus bars carrying thousands of amperes are clamped firmly because the force between parallel currents can bend them during a short-circuit surge.

games.title: Parallel wire facts
items: Two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract.
Opposite to the rule for like charges.
Antiparallel currents attract each other.
They repel.
The force per unit length between parallel wires is inversely proportional to their separation.
The force on the wire with the bigger current is larger.
Newton's third law: the forces are equal and opposite.
Historically, the ampere was defined using the force between parallel wires.
2 × 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹ at 1 m separation.

items.q: Ia = Ib = 1 A, d = 1 m: f (in units of 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹)

learn.hook: Put a current loop in a magnetic field and it twists. That twist turns the shaft of every DC motor and the needle of every analogue meter.
points: Rectangular loop in a uniform field: the forces on opposite sides cancel, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple.
Torque τ = IAB sinθ for one turn, where θ is between the normal to the loop and B. For N turns: τ = NIAB sinθ.
Vector form: τ = m × B, where the magnetic moment m = NIA (unit A m²), directed along the normal by the right-hand rule.
Stable equilibrium when m is parallel to B (θ = 0); unstable when m is antiparallel (θ = 180°). Torque is zero in both.
Torque is maximum (NIAB) when the plane of the loop is parallel to B (θ = 90°).

topics.title: A current loop as a magnetic dipole

learn.hook: A tiny current loop behaves exactly like a tiny bar magnet. In fact, the magnetism of atoms comes from electrons looping around nuclei.
points: Far along the axis (x ≫ R), a loop's field is B = µ₀m/(2πx³) = (µ₀/4π)(2m/x³), where m = IA.
Compare the electric dipole: E = (1/4πε₀)(2p/x³). Swap p → m and 1/ε₀ → µ₀.
A current loop is a magnetic dipole, with north and south faces.
Unlike electric charges, there are no isolated magnetic charges (monopoles): the simplest magnetic element is the current loop (dipole).
Problem toolkit: B of wires, loops and solenoids; force on wires; torque NIAB sinθ; radius mv/(qB).

learn.hook: The swinging needle of an old-school analogue meter is a coil, a magnet and a tiny spring working together, a beautiful use of τ = NIAB.
points: Construction: a coil of N turns on a soft iron core, pivoted between concave pole pieces of a permanent magnet, which make the field radial so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B.
Magnetic torque NIAB is balanced by the spring's restoring torque kφ: kφ = NIAB, so φ = (NAB/k)I. Deflection is proportional to current, giving a linear scale.
Current sensitivity = φ/I = NAB/k (deflection per unit current).
Voltage sensitivity = φ/V = NAB/(kR), where R is the coil resistance.
Doubling N doubles the current sensitivity, but it also doubles R, so the voltage sensitivity stays the same.

topics.title: Converting a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter

learn.hook: A galvanometer is delicate, often going full scale at a few milliamperes. With one well-chosen resistor it becomes a sturdy ammeter or a voltmeter.
points: Ammeter: connect a small shunt resistance S in parallel with the galvanometer (resistance G). Most current bypasses the coil.
Shunt value: S = IgG/(I - Ig), where Ig is the full-scale galvanometer current and I is the required range. The ammeter's resistance is very low, about S.
Voltmeter: connect a large resistance R in series with the galvanometer.
Series value: R = V/Ig - G for a voltmeter of range V. The voltmeter's total resistance is very high.
An ideal ammeter has zero resistance (connected in series); an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance (connected in parallel).

learn.hook: Sailors on the Indian Ocean trade routes trusted the magnetic compass centuries ago. The same lodestone magic now spins hard disks and runs EV motors.
points: Magnetism is found naturally (lodestone). The Earth itself behaves like a huge magnet whose field points roughly from the geographic south to the geographic north, so a freely suspended magnet settles roughly along the north-south line.
Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Cutting a magnet only gives smaller magnets: isolated poles do not exist.
Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet trace a pattern just like that of a current-carrying solenoid.
Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops (outside from N to S, inside from S to N), never intersect, the tangent gives B, and their crowding shows the field's strength.
Unlike electric field lines, which start and end on charges, magnetic field lines have no start or end.

steps: Each piece develops a new N and S at the cut.
Each piece is a complete, weaker magnet.

learn.hook: Cut a solenoid open in your imagination and you will find a bar magnet inside. Their fields are so alike that we use the same formulas for both.
points: A bar magnet behaves like a solenoid: its magnetism comes from tiny circulating currents in its atoms. Its magnetic moment m points along its axis from S to N.
Far field on the axis: B = (µ₀/4π)(2m/r³), along m.
Far field on the equatorial line: B = -(µ₀/4π)(m/r³), opposite to m.
The magnetic moment can be found from the field it produces, or from the torque it feels in a known field (τ = mB sinθ).
A neutral point is where the magnet's field exactly cancels another field (such as Earth's horizontal field); a compass there shows no preferred direction.

topics.title: A magnetic dipole in a uniform field

learn.hook: Flick a compass needle and it oscillates before settling. Count those oscillations and you can actually compare magnetic fields, an old trick of field scientists.
points: A magnetic dipole in uniform B feels no net force but a torque τ = m × B, magnitude mB sinθ, turning m towards B.
Its potential energy is U = -m·B = -mB cosθ: minimum (stable) at θ = 0, maximum (unstable) at θ = 180°.
A compass needle disturbed from equilibrium oscillates; a stronger field gives a stronger restoring torque and faster oscillations, so oscillation rates can compare fields.
Electrostatic analogue: replace p by m and 1/(4πε₀) by µ₀/4π. Then E-dipole formulas give B-dipole formulas.
Analogy table: torque p × E ↔ m × B; energy -p·E ↔ -m·B; axial field 2p/(4πε₀r³) ↔ µ₀2m/(4πr³).

learn.hook: Draw any closed bubble around a magnet, around half a magnet, or around nothing at all. The magnetic flux through it is always exactly zero.
points: Gauss's law for magnetism: the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: ∮B·dS = 0.
Every field line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, because magnetic field lines are closed loops.
This expresses the fact that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist; the simplest magnetic source is a dipole.
Contrast: in electrostatics, ∮E·dS = q/ε₀, which can be non-zero because electric charges exist.
Flux through an open surface (not closed) can be non-zero; the law is only about closed surfaces.

steps: Field lines leave near the north pole...

learn.hook: Slide an iron rod into a solenoid and the field inside can jump hundreds of times. The material itself joins in. Here is how we describe that.
points: Magnetisation M = net magnetic moment per unit volume (unit A m⁻¹).
Magnetic intensity H is defined by B = µ₀(H + M). In a solenoid, H = nI (from the free current), unit A m⁻¹.
For many materials M = χH, where χ (dimensionless) is the magnetic susceptibility. Then B = µ₀(1 + χ)H = µ₀µrH = µH.
Relative permeability µr = 1 + χ; permeability µ = µ₀µr.
χ is small and negative for diamagnets (bismuth about -1.66 × 10⁻⁵), small and positive for paramagnets (aluminium about 2.3 × 10⁻⁵), and very large and positive for ferromagnets.

learn.reallife: Transformer cores at Indian substations use special silicon steel with a very large relative permeability, so a modest current produces a large magnetic flux.

learn.hook: A live frog was once levitated in a strong magnet because water in its body is diamagnetic. Even 'non-magnetic' things respond to magnetic fields.
points: Classification by χ: diamagnetic (χ small, negative), paramagnetic (χ small, positive), ferromagnetic (χ large, positive).
Diamagnets are weakly repelled; they move from stronger to weaker field regions, and field lines are slightly pushed out of them. Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water, nitrogen at STP.
Superconductors cooled below their critical temperature expel the field completely (χ = -1, µr = 0): the Meissner effect. They are perfect diamagnets.
Paramagnets have atoms with permanent magnetic moments. A field partly aligns them against thermal randomness, so they are weakly attracted, moving from weak to strong field regions.
Examples of paramagnets: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen at STP, copper chloride.

example.q: A bar of bismuth and a bar of aluminium are hung freely between the poles of a strong magnet. How do they settle?
steps: Bismuth is diamagnetic, so it moves away from the strongest field.

example.answer: Bismuth across the field; aluminium along the field

learn.hook: Why is iron so dramatically magnetic while aluminium barely notices a magnet? The answer lies in tiny regions called domains.
points: In ferromagnets (iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium), atomic moments line up spontaneously in small regions called domains, each about 1 mm across.
Normally domains point randomly. An applied field grows the domains aligned with it and rotates others, giving a huge M and very large χ; they are strongly attracted.
Hard ferromagnets (alnico, used for permanent magnets) keep their magnetisation; soft ferromagnets (soft iron, used in electromagnets and transformer cores) lose it when the field is removed.
Above a certain temperature, the Curie temperature, a ferromagnet loses its ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic.
Problem tips: sign of χ classifies the material; in a non-uniform field, ferromagnets and paramagnets move to stronger fields, diamagnets to weaker fields.

example.q: An iron nail is attracted to a magnet but loses that property after strong heating. Explain.
steps: Iron is ferromagnetic because of aligned domains.
Heating above the Curie temperature destroys the spontaneous alignment.
The nail becomes paramagnetic, only weakly attracted.
example.answer: Heating above the Curie temperature makes iron lose its ferromagnetism

learn.reallife: Permanent magnets in the motors of Indian-made electric two-wheelers are hard ferromagnets, while the cores of electromagnets in scrapyard cranes in Alang are soft iron.

learn.hook: Oersted showed currents make magnetism. Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry asked the reverse: can magnetism make a current? Their answer powers every home in India.
points: Electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field (more precisely, a changing magnetic flux) produces an emf and a current in a circuit.
It underlies generators in power plants, transformers, induction cooktops and wireless charging.
Experiment 1: moving a bar magnet towards or away from a coil connected to a galvanometer deflects it. Faster motion gives a larger deflection; no motion, no deflection.
Experiment 2: moving a current-carrying coil towards or away from a second coil induces a current in the second coil.
Experiment 3: with both coils stationary, switching the current in one coil on or off induces a brief current in the other. A steady current induces nothing.

example.q: A magnet is held still inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. What does the galvanometer show? What if the magnet is pulled out quickly?
steps: Stationary magnet: flux through the coil is constant, so no emf.
Pulling it out changes the flux quickly.
example.answer: No deflection when still; a large deflection while it is pulled out quickly

learn.reallife: Every unit of electricity reaching Indian homes from Bhakra Nangal, Tehri or NTPC's coal plants is produced by electromagnetic induction in giant generators.

learn.hook: All of Faraday's experiments had one thing in common: the number of magnetic field lines through the coil was changing. Physicists call it magnetic flux.
points: Faraday's conclusion: an induced emf appears whenever the magnetic flux through a circuit changes.
Magnetic flux through a plane area A in a uniform field: Φ = B·A = BA cosθ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area.
For a non-uniform field: Φ = Σ B·dA (sum over small elements).
Flux is a scalar. SI unit: weber (Wb), 1 Wb = 1 T m².
Flux can be changed in three ways: change B, change the area A, or change the angle θ (rotate the coil).

example.q: A square loop of side 10 cm is in a field of 0.5 T, with its normal at 60° to B. Find Φ.

learn.reallife: Induction cooktops sold across India change the magnetic flux through the pan's base 20,000 or more times a second, so currents swirl in the metal and heat it.

teach.praise: Chirp! Φ = BA cosθ, so change B, A or θ to change the flux. Three knobs to turn!

learn.hook: The emf you get does not depend on how much flux there is, but on how fast it changes. Faraday turned that idea into a law with one simple equation.
points: Faraday's law: the induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt.
For a coil of N turns: ε = -N dΦ/dt. Average emf ε = -NΔΦ/Δt.
Induced current I = ε/R, and the charge that flows Q = NΔΦ/R (independent of how fast the change happens).
Example: pulling a square loop out of a field region changes Φ from BA to 0; the emf depends on how quickly it is removed.
The minus sign expresses Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change.

example.q: A 50-turn coil of area 0.02 m² is perpendicular to a field that drops from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.2 s. Find the average emf.
steps: ΔΦ per turn = ΔB × A = 0.4 × 0.02 = 8 × 10⁻³ Wb

learn.reallife: Electromagnetic flow meters used by Indian water utilities measure flow speed from the emf induced in moving water as it crosses a magnetic field, a direct use of Faraday's law.

learn.hook: Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and it falls in eerie slow motion. Lenz's law is pushing back.
points: Lenz's law: the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
This is a consequence of conservation of energy: you must do work against the opposing force, and that work becomes electrical energy (and heat).
If the induced current helped the change, energy would appear from nothing, which is impossible.
Magnet's N pole approaching a coil: the coil's near face becomes a north pole (repels). N pole moving away: the near face becomes south (attracts).
A loop leaving a field region: the induced current tries to keep the flux, so its own field is in the same direction as the external field.

example.q: A magnet's north pole is pushed towards a coil. Seen from the magnet's side, what is the direction of the induced current?
steps: The coil opposes it by making its near face a north pole.
A north face, seen from outside, has an anticlockwise current.
example.answer: Anticlockwise, as seen from the magnet's side

learn.reallife: Electromagnetic brakes on some metro trains, like Delhi Metro's regenerative systems, use induction: the induced currents oppose the motion, slowing the train and feeding energy back to the grid.

quiz.q: A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls slowly because
options: currents induced in the tube oppose its motion (Lenz's law)
air resistance in the tube is high
quiz.explain: As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring of the tube changes, inducing currents whose magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law).

quiz.q: The field through a loop points upward and is increasing. The induced current produces a field that, inside the loop, points
quiz.explain: To oppose the increase of upward flux, the induced field points down.
quiz.mistake: Points the induced field along the existing field

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pushing a magnet into a coil requires more effort when the coil's ends are joined than when they are open. Reason (R): With the ends joined, an induced current flows and opposes the motion. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With an open circuit there is an emf but no current, so no opposing magnetic force.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the emf alone exerts the force

quiz.q: A metal ring is placed around the top of a vertical solenoid. When the current in the solenoid is switched on, the ring
options: jumps up, repelled by the solenoid
quiz.explain: The increasing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes it, so the ring is repelled (the jumping ring experiment).

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the induced current always fight the change? Is it just being stubborn?'
teach.praise: Chirp! If it helped, energy would come from nowhere. Opposing the change keeps energy conserved: work in, electricity out!
teach.nudge: Good! Which conservation law would be broken if the induced current helped the change?

learn.hook: Slide a metal rod across two rails in a magnetic field and a voltage appears between its ends, no battery needed. It is the simplest generator possible.
points: A rod of length l moving at speed v perpendicular to a uniform B, on rails forming a loop: area changes at rate lv, so ε = Blv.
Explanation with Lorentz force: each free charge in the rod feels qvB along the rod, pushing charges to one end; the work per unit charge over length l is vBl.
If the circuit has resistance R, current I = Blv/R flows, and the rod feels a retarding force F = BIl = B²l²v/R.
To keep the rod at constant speed, an external force must supply power P = Fv = B²l²v²/R, which equals the electrical power I²R dissipated. Energy is conserved.
The direction of the induced current can be found by Fleming's right-hand rule or by Lenz's law.

example.q: A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.2 T field on rails with R = 2 Ω. Find ε, I and the force needed.

learn.reallife: When a Vande Bharat train speeds along, its steel axle is a long conductor moving through Earth's magnetic field, so a small motional emf exists between the ends of the axle.

games.title: Energy flow in a sliding rod
items: External agent pulls the rod
Rod's motion changes the flux and induces emf Blv
Current I = Blv/R flows
Field exerts a retarding force BIl on the rod
Work done by the agent appears as I²R heat

B = 0.5 T, l = 0.2 m, v = 10 m s⁻¹: ε (in V)

quiz.mistake: Gives the force instead of power

quiz.q: In terms of the Lorentz force, the emf in a moving rod arises because
options: free charges in the rod feel a force q(v × B) along the rod
the field does work on the charges directly
quiz.explain: This force pushes charges to the ends and does work vBl per unit charge.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rod becomes a magnet

quiz.q: If the speed of the rod is doubled, the power needed to keep it moving (resistance fixed) becomes
quiz.explain: P = B²l²v²/R ∝ v².
quiz.mistake: Thinks power is proportional to v

quiz.q: A rod slides on rails in a field. If the circuit is broken (open rails), then
options: an emf exists but no current flows and no retarding force acts
quiz.explain: The emf Blv still appears, but without a closed path there is no current.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an emf always needs a current

quiz.explain: v × B = 0 when v is parallel to B.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does the energy come from when a sliding rod lights a bulb?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The pusher does work against a retarding force BIl, and that work becomes the bulb's energy. Energy conserved!
teach.nudge: Good! What force acts on the rod once current flows, and who has to overcome it?

topics.title: Rotating rods, wheels and moving vehicles

learn.hook: An aeroplane's metal wings, a spinning bicycle wheel and a train's axle all cut Earth's magnetic field. Each one is a tiny, unintended generator.
points: A metal rod of length l rotating with angular speed ω about one end, perpendicular to B: different parts move at different speeds (v = ωr). Total ε = ½Bωl².
A metal wheel spinning in an axial field has the same emf between its centre (axle) and rim: ε = ½BωR².
A plane flying horizontally: its wings cut the vertical component of Earth's field, so ε = B_vertical × wingspan × speed.
A train moving on level tracks: its axle (length l) cuts the vertical component, so ε = B_vertical × l × v.
Exercise toolkit: ε = -NdΦ/dt, ε = Blv, ε = ½Bωl², ε = -L dI/dt and ε = -M dI/dt.

example.q: A 0.8 m metal rod rotates at 250 rad s⁻¹ about one end in a field of 0.4 T along its axis of rotation. Find the emf between its ends.

learn.reallife: A passenger jet with a 34 m wingspan flying at 250 m s⁻¹ over north India, where the vertical component of Earth's field is about 3 × 10⁻⁵ T, has roughly 0.26 V across its wingtips. It cannot drive a current because the whole plane moves together.

Average speed along the rod is ωl/2.
A horizontally flying aircraft's wings cut the horizontal component of Earth's field.
It is the vertical component that matters.
Doubling the length of a rotating rod doubles its emf.
ε ∝ l², so it becomes four times.
A spinning bicycle wheel in a magnetic field has an emf between its axle and rim.
Each spoke acts like a rotating rod.
Doubling the angular speed doubles the emf of a rotating rod.

Because only half the rod is in the field
Because the rod rotates only half a turn
quiz.explain: Summing B(ωr)dr from 0 to l gives ½Bωl².
quiz.mistake: Uses the tip speed for the whole rod

quiz.q: Which component of Earth's magnetic field causes an emf across the wings of a plane flying horizontally?
quiz.explain: The wings move horizontally, so only the vertical component is perpendicular to both v and the wing.

quiz.q: A coil of 100 turns has its flux changed by 0.02 Wb per turn in 0.4 s. What is the emf (in V)?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'A spinning rod's tip moves fastest. Why is its emf ½Bωl²?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Speed grows from zero at the centre to ωl at the tip, so the average is ωl/2, giving ½Bωl². Spin-tastic!
teach.nudge: Good! Do all parts of the rod move at the same speed?

learn.hook: Wireless phone chargers, Indian Railways track circuits and every transformer rely on one coil 'talking' to another through changing flux. That link is mutual inductance.
points: For a coil near a current, flux linkage NΦ is proportional to the current. The constant of proportionality is the inductance.
Inductance depends only on the geometry of the coils (turns, size, separation) and the medium (permeability). SI unit: henry (H), 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹.
Mutual inductance: N₁Φ₁ = M₁₂I₂, the flux in coil 1 due to current in coil 2. It can be shown that M₁₂ = M₂₁ = M.
Two long coaxial solenoids (inner radius r₁, length l, turns per metre n₁ and n₂): M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l. With a core of µr, M is multiplied by µr.
Induced emf in one coil due to changing current in the other: ε₁ = -M dI₂/dt.

example.q: Two coils have M = 0.2 H. The current in coil 2 rises from 0 to 5 A in 0.1 s. Find the emf in coil 1.

learn.reallife: Wireless chargers for phones sold in Indian markets put a transmitter coil and a receiver coil close together; the larger their mutual inductance, the better the charging.

games.title: Mutual inductance
items: Mutual inductance depends on the currents flowing in the coils.
It depends only on geometry and medium.
The mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 equals that of coil 2 with respect to coil 1.
M₁₂ = M₂₁.
Moving two coils further apart reduces their mutual inductance.
Less flux links them.
A steady current in one coil induces a steady emf in the other.
Only a changing current induces emf.
Inserting a soft iron core increases mutual inductance.
M is multiplied by µr.

quiz.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 1.5 H. The current in one changes at 4 A s⁻¹. What emf is induced in the other (in V)?
A current change from 2 A to 8 A in 0.3 s in coil A induces an average emf of 12 V in coil B. What is M (in H)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the final current instead of the change

quiz.q: Two long coaxial solenoids are each 1 m long. The inner one has radius 2 cm and 1000 turns per metre; the outer has 500 turns per metre. What is M (in mH)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, π = 3.14)
quiz.mistake: Uses the outer radius or forgets π in the area

quiz.q: Which is equivalent to one henry?
quiz.explain: From ε = M dI/dt, M = ε/(dI/dt) has units V/(A s⁻¹) = V s A⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Gets the time unit upside down

quiz.q: Inductance of a pair of coils depends on
options: the rate of change of current only
their geometry, separation and the medium around them
quiz.explain: M is a geometric and material property, like capacitance.

quiz.q: A soft iron core of µr = 500 is put inside a pair of coaxial solenoids with M = 2 mH (in air). What is M now (in H)?
Two coils are placed with their planes perpendicular and centres together. Compared with coaxial placement, their mutual inductance is
quiz.explain: The field of one coil hardly threads the other when they are perpendicular.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mutual inductance between two coils is the same whichever coil carries the current. Reason (R): M₁₂ = M₂₁ for any pair of coils. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: This reciprocity holds generally, so the induced emf per unit rate of change is the same both ways.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger coil always has a larger M

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a current in one coil create a voltage in another coil that it does not touch?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A changing current in one coil changes the flux through the other, inducing ε = -M dI/dt. No touching needed!
teach.nudge: Good! What must be changing, and what quantity links the two coils?

topics.title: Self-inductance and energy in an inductor

learn.hook: Switch off a large motor and you may see a spark at the switch. The coil fights the sudden drop in its own current with a burst of back emf.
points: Self-inductance: a coil's own flux linkage NΦ = LI. Changing I induces an emf in the same coil: ε = -L dI/dt (back emf).
The back emf opposes any change in current, rising or falling. An inductor plays the role in circuits that mass (inertia) plays in mechanics.
Long solenoid of n turns per metre, area A and length l: L = µ₀n²Al. With a core: L = µrµ₀n²Al.
Energy stored in an inductor: U = ½LI², analogous to kinetic energy ½mv².

Mutual inductance examples: for long coaxial solenoids M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l; for a small loop of radius r₁ at the centre of a large coplanar loop of radius r₂ (r₁ ≪ r₂), the large loop's field µ₀I/(2r₂) is nearly uniform over the small loop, so M = µ₀πr₁²/(2r₂).

example.q: A 0.5 H inductor carries 4 A. Find the stored energy. If the current falls to zero in 0.01 s, what average back emf appears?

learn.reallife: Tube lights in older Indian homes used a choke (an inductor). Its large back emf when the starter opened gave the high voltage spike needed to strike the tube.

games.title: Mechanics and inductors
pairs: Back emf opposes change in current

items.q: L = 2 H, dI/dt = 3 A s⁻¹: |ε| (in V)
L = 0.1 H, I = 10 A: energy (in J)
L = 4 H, I = 1 A: energy (in J)
|ε| = 10 V, dI/dt = 5 A s⁻¹: L (in H)

An inductor of 2 H carries 3 A. How much energy is stored in it (in J)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ or the square

quiz.q: A solenoid has 1000 turns per metre, cross-section 10⁻³ m² and length 0.5 m. What is its self-inductance (in mH)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷, π = 3.14)
The number of turns per unit length of a solenoid is doubled (same size). Its self-inductance becomes
quiz.explain: L ∝ n².

quiz.q: A small circular loop of radius r₁ lies at the centre of a much larger coplanar circular loop of radius r₂ (r₁ ≪ r₂). What is their mutual inductance?
quiz.explain: A current I in the large loop gives B = µ₀I/(2r₂) at its centre, almost uniform over the small loop. Flux through the small loop = πr₁² × µ₀I/(2r₂), so M = Φ/I = µ₀πr₁²/(2r₂).
steps: Field at centre of large loop: B = µ₀I/(2r₂)
Flux through small loop: Φ = B × πr₁² = µ₀Iπr₁²/(2r₂)
quiz.mistake: Uses the area of the large loop instead of the small loop, or forgets the factor 2 in the loop-centre field

quiz.q: A coil's current rises from 0 to 2 A in 0.05 s, and the average back emf is 8 V. What is L (in H)?
Why does a spark often appear at a switch when the current in a large inductive coil is suddenly cut?
options: The coil stores charge like a capacitor
The switch has very high resistance
The rapid fall in current induces a large back emf that opposes the drop
quiz.explain: |ε| = L dI/dt is large when dI/dt is large.
quiz.mistake: Confuses an inductor with a capacitor

quiz.q: An inductor's role in a circuit is analogous to which quantity in mechanics?
quiz.explain: It resists changes in current as mass resists changes in velocity.

quiz.q: The energy stored in an inductor is 8 J when the current is 2 A. What is the energy when the current is 4 A (in J)?
quiz.explain: U ∝ I²: doubling I gives 4 × 8 = 32 J.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the energy instead of quadrupling

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a coil push back when I try to change its current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A changing current changes the coil's own flux, inducing a back emf -L dI/dt that opposes the change. Like inertia!
teach.nudge: Good! What does a coil induce in itself when its current changes, and which way does it act?

learn.hook: At Tehri dam, falling water spins turbines that turn huge coils in magnetic fields. The flux through each coil swings back and forth 50 times every second.
points: Principle: a coil rotating in a uniform magnetic field has a continuously changing flux Φ = NBA cos ωt.
Induced emf ε = NBAω sin ωt. Peak emf ε₀ = NBAω; it is zero when the coil's plane is perpendicular to B and maximum when the plane is parallel to B.
Construction: armature coil, strong field magnets, slip rings that rotate with the coil, and carbon brushes that press on the rings to take the current out.
In hydroelectric plants, falling water turns the turbines; in thermal plants, steam does it. The generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
India's mains frequency is 50 Hz, so ω = 2π × 50 ≈ 314 rad s⁻¹.

example.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.05 m² rotates at 50 rev s⁻¹ in a 0.02 T field. Find the peak emf. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: The grid frequency monitored by Grid-India stays very close to 50 Hz; if generators slow down under heavy load, the frequency dips and control centres respond in seconds.

games.title: How a hydro generator delivers power
items: Water falls through the penstock
Water spins the turbine
Turbine rotates the coil in a magnetic field
Changing flux induces an alternating emf
Slip rings and brushes deliver current to the grid

games.title: Generator facts
items: Peak emf of a generator is NBAω.
From ε = NBAω sin ωt.
The emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B.
Flux is maximum then, but its rate of change is zero.
Slip rings rotate with the armature coil.
Brushes stay fixed and press on them.
Doubling the speed of rotation doubles both the peak emf and the frequency.
ε₀ = NBAω and ν = ω/2π.
The mains frequency in India is 60 Hz.
It is 50 Hz.

quiz.q: A coil of 50 turns and area 0.2 m² rotates at ω = 100 rad s⁻¹ in a field of 0.05 T. What is the peak emf (in V)?
A generator's peak emf is 200 V. If its speed of rotation is halved, the new peak emf is (in V)
quiz.explain: ε₀ ∝ ω.
quiz.mistake: Thinks peak emf depends on ω²

quiz.q: At what position of the rotating coil is the induced emf maximum?
options: When the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
When the flux through the coil is maximum
At no position; it is constant
quiz.explain: Then flux is zero but changing fastest, since ε ∝ sin ωt.
quiz.mistake: Confuses maximum flux with maximum emf

quiz.q: A 200-turn coil of area 0.05 m² rotates at 50 rev s⁻¹ in a 0.1 T field. What is the peak emf (in V)? (π = 3.14)
What is the function of the slip rings and brushes in an AC generator?
options: To connect the rotating coil to the external circuit without twisting the wires
quiz.explain: The rings turn with the coil while the stationary brushes slide on them.
quiz.mistake: Confuses slip rings with a split-ring commutator

quiz.q: The emf of a generator is ε = 300 sin(314t) V. What is its frequency (in Hz)? (π = 3.14)
quiz.mistake: Takes ω itself as the frequency

quiz.q: In a thermal power plant, the turbines that turn the generators are driven by
quiz.explain: Burning coal boils water; the steam drives the turbines.

quiz.q: A generator converts
quiz.explain: Work done to rotate the coil against the magnetic opposing force becomes electrical energy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a generator with a motor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a spinning coil make alternating current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! As the coil spins, the flux changes as cos ωt, so the emf is NBAω sin ωt, flipping direction every half turn. AC!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the flux as the coil rotates, and what shape is the emf?

learn.hook: The socket in your room does not give a steady push. Its voltage swings from +311 V to -311 V and back fifty times every second.
points: Alternating voltage varies sinusoidally with time: v = vm sin ωt, where vm is the peak value and ω = 2πν. Most power supplies in homes and industry are AC.
AC is preferred because transformers can easily step its voltage up or down, which makes long-distance transmission efficient.
Across a resistor R, i = (vm/R) sin ωt = im sin ωt: the current is in phase with the voltage.
Over a full cycle, the average current is zero (equal positive and negative halves), but the power i²R is always positive, so the average power is not zero.
Average power in a resistor: P = ½im²R, because the average of sin²ωt over a cycle is ½.

example.q: A 50 Ω resistor is connected to v = 100 sin(314t) V. Find the peak current and the average power.

learn.reallife: Electric geysers and irons in Indian homes are essentially resistors. They heat up on AC just as on DC because heating depends on i², which is positive in both halves of each cycle.

games.title: AC in a resistor
items: In a pure resistor, current and voltage are in phase.
Both are proportional to sin ωt.
The average AC current over a full cycle is zero.
Positive and negative halves cancel.
The average power in a resistor on AC is zero.
i²R is never negative, so the average is ½im²R.
AC can be stepped up or down using transformers.
This is its key advantage.
The average of sin²ωt over one cycle is 1.
It is ½.

items.q: vm = 200 V, R = 100 Ω: im (in A)
im = 2 A, R = 10 Ω: average power (in W)
Average of sin²ωt over a cycle
ω for 50 Hz, taking π = 3.14 (in rad s⁻¹)
Phase difference between v and i in R (in degrees)

quiz.q: A voltage v = 220 sin(100πt) V is applied to a 44 Ω resistor. What is the peak current (in A)?
What is the frequency of v = 220 sin(100πt) V (in Hz)?
quiz.explain: ω = 100π = 2πν, so ν = 50 Hz.
quiz.mistake: Takes the coefficient of t as the frequency

quiz.q: A resistor of 20 Ω carries an AC current of peak value 3 A. What is the average power (in W)?
The average value of an alternating current over one complete cycle is
quiz.explain: The positive half cancels the negative half.

quiz.q: Why is the average power in a resistor on AC not zero, though the average current is zero?
options: Power depends on i², which is positive in both halves of the cycle
Because AC has no negative half
quiz.explain: i²R ≥ 0 at every instant.

quiz.q: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the phase difference between current and voltage is
quiz.explain: Both vary as sin ωt.
quiz.mistake: Confuses resistor with inductor or capacitor

quiz.q: Which is the main reason AC is used for power distribution rather than DC?
options: Its voltage can be changed easily and efficiently using transformers
quiz.explain: High-voltage transmission with step-up and step-down transformers reduces losses.
quiz.mistake: Thinks AC is safer by nature

quiz.q: A 100 Ω resistor dissipates 50 W on AC. What is the peak current (in A)?
quiz.explain: P = ½im²R gives im² = 2P/R = 1, so im = 1 A.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If AC current averages to zero, how does my geyser get hot?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Heating goes as i²R, which is positive in both halves, so average power is ½im²R. Hot water!
teach.nudge: Good! Does heating depend on i or on i²?

learn.hook: Your meter says 220 V, but the voltage actually peaks at about 311 V. The 220 is a special average called the root mean square.
points: RMS (effective) current I = im/√2 ≈ 0.707im, and RMS voltage V = vm/√2. The AC gives the same heating as a DC of this value: P = VI = I²R.
AC ammeters and voltmeters read RMS values. Indian mains of 220 V (RMS) has a peak of 220√2 ≈ 311 V.
A phasor is a vector that rotates anticlockwise at angular speed ω; its projection on the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value (vm sin ωt).
Phasor diagrams show the phase relation between voltage and current: in a resistor, the V and I phasors point the same way.
Phasors for different circuit elements add as vectors, which makes AC circuit analysis simple.

example.q: A 100 W bulb is rated for 220 V. Find its RMS current and peak current. (√2 = 1.414)

learn.reallife: A multimeter in a Delhi electrician's kit reading 230 V on a socket is reporting the RMS value; the voltage actually peaks near 325 V.

items.text: A phasor rotates ___ at angular speed ω.

For a resistor, V and I phasors are ___.

quiz.q: The peak value of an alternating current is 10 A. What is its RMS value (in A)? (√2 = 1.414)
The RMS voltage of a supply is 230 V. What is its peak voltage (in V)? (√2 = 1.414)
An AC voltmeter connected to the Indian mains reads 220 V. This is the
quiz.explain: AC meters are calibrated to show RMS values.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the meter reads the peak

quiz.q: A 60 W bulb runs on 240 V AC. What is the RMS current (in A)?
An AC of RMS value 2 A flows through 50 Ω. What average power is dissipated (in W)?
quiz.explain: P = I²R using RMS current: 4 × 50 = 200 W.
quiz.mistake: Applies the ½ to an RMS value

quiz.q: What does the projection of a voltage phasor on the vertical axis represent?
quiz.explain: Projection = vm sin ωt, the value at that instant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the phasor length changes with time

quiz.q: A phasor diagram for a pure resistor shows V and I phasors that are
quiz.explain: Voltage and current are in phase in R.

quiz.q: A DC current of 3 A produces the same heating in a resistor as an AC of peak value (in A)? (√2 = 1.414)
quiz.explain: Equal heating means RMS = 3 A, so im = 3√2 ≈ 4.24 A.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the meter say 220 V if the voltage actually reaches 311 V?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The meter shows RMS, the DC value that gives the same heating, which is peak/√2. 311/1.414 ≈ 220!
teach.nudge: Good! What does RMS mean, and how is it related to the peak value?

learn.hook: Put an inductor on AC and something strange happens: the current always reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the voltage. The coil makes the current lag.
points: For v = vm sin ωt across inductance L: i = im sin(ωt - π/2). The current lags the voltage by π/2 (90°).
Inductive reactance XL = ωL = 2πνL, unit ohm. Peak current im = vm/XL, and RMS I = V/XL.
XL increases with frequency: an inductor lets DC (ω = 0) pass freely but opposes high-frequency AC.
Average power over a cycle in a pure inductor is zero: energy is stored in its field in one quarter cycle and returned in the next.
The opposition comes from the back emf L di/dt, not from any resistance.

learn.hook: A capacitor blocks DC completely, yet an AC current seems to flow 'through' it. Charges simply rush on and off the plates every half cycle.
points: For v = vm sin ωt across capacitance C: i = im sin(ωt + π/2). The current leads the voltage by π/2 (90°).
Capacitive reactance XC = 1/(ωC) = 1/(2πνC), unit ohm. Peak current im = vm/XC.
XC decreases with frequency. For DC (ω = 0), XC is infinite, so a capacitor blocks DC.
Average power over a cycle in a pure capacitor is zero.
A lamp in series with a capacitor glows brighter if C or the frequency is increased (XC falls, current rises).

learn.hook: Radio sets, induction furnaces and the power-factor panels in Indian factories all contain resistors, inductors and capacitors in series. Phasors make them easy.
points: In series, the same current flows through R, L and C. VR is in phase with I, VL leads I by 90°, VC lags I by 90°.
Phasor sum: Vm² = VRm² + (VCm - VLm)², so the impedance is Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²), with vm = imZ.
Impedance diagram: R along one axis and (XC - XL) at right angles; Z is the hypotenuse.
Phase angle: tanφ = (XC - XL)/R. If XL > XC the circuit is inductive (current lags); if XC > XL it is capacitive (current leads).
Individual voltages VR = IR, VL = IXL, VC = IXC can be larger than the supply voltage, because they are not in phase.

example.q: R = 30 Ω, XL = 80 Ω, XC = 40 Ω in series across 100 V (RMS). Find Z, I and VR, VL, VC.
steps: VR = 60 V, VL = 160 V, VC = 80 V
example.answer: Z = 50 Ω; I = 2 A; VR = 60 V, VL = 160 V, VC = 80 V

learn.hook: Turn the tuning knob of an old FM radio and one station suddenly comes in loud and clear. You have just made an LCR circuit resonate.
points: Resonance occurs when XL = XC, i.e. ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C), so ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
At resonance Z = R (minimum) and the current is maximum, im = vm/R. Current and voltage are in phase.
A graph of current against frequency peaks at ω₀. Smaller R gives a taller, sharper peak; larger R gives a flatter peak.
Resonance needs both L and C; an RL or RC circuit cannot resonate.
Radio tuning: changing C shifts ω₀ to match a station's frequency, so that station's signal produces the largest current.

topics.title: Power in AC circuits and power factor

learn.hook: Electricity boards in India charge factories a penalty if their power factor is low. A bank of capacitors can save lakhs of rupees a year.
points: Average power in an AC circuit: P = VI cosφ (V and I are RMS), where φ is the phase difference. cosφ is the power factor.
Pure resistor: φ = 0, cosφ = 1, P = VI. Pure inductor or capacitor: φ = ±90°, cosφ = 0, P = 0. Such current is called wattless current.
Series LCR: cosφ = R/Z. At resonance Z = R, so cosφ = 1 and power is maximum.
A low power factor means a large current for the same useful power, so I²R losses in the lines rise.
Industries add capacitors to cancel the lagging current drawn by motors (inductive loads), raising the power factor towards 1.

example.q: A circuit with R = 60 Ω and Z = 100 Ω is connected to 200 V RMS. Find the power factor and the average power.

learn.reallife: State electricity boards, from Maharashtra's MSEDCL to Tamil Nadu's TANGEDCO, set minimum power factor rules for industrial consumers, which is why factories install capacitor banks.

learn.hook: A phone charger steps 230 V down to about 5 V. The power station steps it up to 400 kV. Both use the same simple device: two coils and an iron core.
points: Principle: mutual induction. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing flux in a soft iron core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil.
Ideal transformer: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, and with no losses VpIp = VsIs, so Ip/Is = Ns/Np.
Step-up transformer: Ns > Np (voltage raised, current lowered). Step-down transformer: Ns < Np.

Energy losses: flux leakage (reduced by winding coils on top of each other), resistance of windings (thick copper wire), eddy currents in the core (laminated core) and hysteresis (soft iron with a narrow loop).
A transformer works only with AC (or changing current); steady DC gives no changing flux.

example.q: A step-down transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. With 220 V on the primary, find Vs. If the secondary delivers 10 A, find Ip (ideal).

learn.reallife: The grey transformer on an electric pole in an Indian neighbourhood steps 11 kV down to about 415 V between phases (three-phase), which gives about 230-240 V between a phase and neutral for each home.

topics.title: Power transmission and AC problem solving

learn.hook: Electricity from a hydro plant in Himachal reaches homes in Delhi hundreds of kilometres away. Transformers at both ends make that journey efficient.
points: Power is generated at about 11 to 25 kV, stepped up to hundreds of kV for long-distance lines, then stepped down at substations (to 33 kV, 11 kV and finally 230 V).
For a fixed power P = VI, raising V lowers I, and the line loss I²R falls as 1/V².
Problem example: an ideal step-up transformer from 11 kV to 220 kV has Ns/Np = 20; the line current is 1/20 of the generator current.
Toolkit: V = vm/√2; XL = ωL; XC = 1/(ωC); Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²); ω₀ = 1/√(LC); P = VI cosφ; Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
Always check whether values given are peak or RMS before using them in formulas.

topics.title: Maxwell's prediction and the first EM waves

learn.hook: Long before Wi-Fi and 5G, a Scottish physicist doing algebra on paper predicted invisible waves that travel at the speed of light. A few decades later, they were found.
points: Faraday showed a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Maxwell asked: does a changing electric field produce a magnetic field? He concluded it does.
Maxwell's equations then predicted electromagnetic (EM) waves of linked, changing E and B fields, travelling at about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹: the speed of light. So light itself is an EM wave.
In 1887 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected EM waves in the laboratory, confirming Maxwell.
Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata produced and studied EM waves of much shorter wavelength (about 25 mm to 5 mm).
Guglielmo Marconi transmitted EM waves over many kilometres, opening the era of radio communication.

example.q: Why was Maxwell's calculated speed of EM waves such a big deal?
steps: His theory gave the wave speed as 1/√(µ₀ε₀).
This came out equal to the measured speed of light.
So light must be an electromagnetic wave.
example.answer: It showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, uniting optics with electricity and magnetism

learn.reallife: J.C. Bose's millimetre-wave work at Presidency College, Kolkata, in the 1890s anticipated technologies now used in 5G and car radar.

learn.hook: While a capacitor charges, current flows in the wires but no charge crosses the gap. Yet a compass placed near the gap still feels a magnetic field. Maxwell found the missing current.
points: Ampere's law fails while a capacitor charges: a loop around the wire gives ∮B·dl = µ₀i through a flat surface, but zero through a surface passing between the plates. The results contradict each other.
Between the plates, the electric flux ΦE changes. Maxwell defined displacement current id = ε₀ dΦE/dt.
Ampere-Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(ic + ε₀ dΦE/dt) = µ₀(ic + id).
The total current (conduction + displacement) is continuous: in the wires it is all ic, in the gap it is all id, and they are equal.
So a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.

example.q: A capacitor is being charged by a current of 2 A. What is the displacement current between its plates?
steps: Charge on plate q = ε₀EA = ε₀ΦE

learn.reallife: Electrical engineers designing high-frequency circuits for ISRO's satellites must account for displacement currents through capacitors and even through the air gaps between conductors.

topics.title: Maxwell's equations and how EM waves are made

learn.hook: Four short equations describe every electric and magnetic phenomenon, from a static zap to a 5G signal. The fourth one makes waves possible.
points: Maxwell's equations: (1) Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀; (2) Gauss's law for magnetism ∮B·dA = 0; (3) Faraday's law ∮E·dl = -dΦB/dt; (4) Ampere-Maxwell law ∮B·dl = µ₀ic + µ₀ε₀ dΦE/dt. Plus the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B).
Stationary charges make only E; charges in uniform motion (steady currents) make steady B; but accelerated charges radiate EM waves.
An oscillating charge (for example in an antenna) produces an oscillating E, which produces an oscillating B, and so on: the wave carries away energy at the charge's frequency.
In an EM wave, E and B oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel: EM waves are transverse.
E, B and the direction of propagation follow the order E × B, giving the direction the wave travels.

example.q: An electron oscillates in an antenna at 100 MHz. What frequency does the radiated wave have, and why?
steps: The fields oscillate at the same frequency as the charge.
So the wave frequency is 100 MHz.
example.answer: 100 MHz, the frequency of the oscillating charge

learn.reallife: The tall masts of Doordarshan and All India Radio have antennas in which electrons are made to oscillate; these accelerated charges launch the waves your TV or radio picks up.

topics.title: Nature and properties of EM waves

learn.hook: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to cross 150 million km of empty space, carrying enough energy to power the solar parks of Rajasthan and to push on solar sails.
points: For a wave travelling along z: Ex = E₀ sin(kz - ωt), By = B₀ sin(kz - ωt), with k = 2π/λ and ω = 2πν. E and B are in phase.
Speed in vacuum: c = ω/k = νλ = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. In a medium: v = 1/√(µε).
The amplitudes are related: E₀/B₀ = c (and E/B = c at every instant).
EM waves need no medium. They carry energy and momentum; on absorption they exert radiation pressure. Momentum delivered p = U/c for total absorption.
Example: a wave with B₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁸ T has E₀ = cB₀ = 6 V m⁻¹.

example.q: A plane EM wave of frequency 30 MHz travels in vacuum along x. At some point E = 9 ĵ V m⁻¹. Find B there.
steps: Direction: E × B must point along +x, and ĵ × k̂ = î, so B is along +z (k̂)

learn.reallife: ISRO's solar panels on satellites and India's solar parks absorb sunlight energy; the same light also delivers a tiny momentum, which spacecraft designers must account for over long missions.

topics.title: EM spectrum: radio, microwave and infrared

learn.hook: Your FM radio, the microwave oven warming leftover biryani and the TV remote are all using light that your eyes cannot see.
points: The EM spectrum is arranged by frequency or wavelength. The regions overlap; there are no sharp boundaries.
Radio waves (λ > 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in antennas. AM band 530 kHz to 1710 kHz; FM band 88 MHz to 108 MHz; TV bands from 54 MHz up to 890 MHz; mobile phones use UHF.

Microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm): produced by special vacuum tubes such as klystrons and magnetrons, and Gunn diodes. Used in radar for aircraft navigation and in microwave ovens, where they heat food by agitating water molecules.

Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): 'heat waves', given out by hot bodies and vibrating molecules. Used in TV remotes, night vision, physiotherapy heat lamps, and the greenhouse effect warms Earth by trapping IR.
Infrared is detected by thermopiles and bolometers, and many snakes can sense it.

example.q: A station broadcasts at 98.3 MHz. Which band and roughly what wavelength?

learn.reallife: Doppler weather radars run by the India Meteorological Department use microwaves to track cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and monsoon rain bands.

topics.title: EM spectrum: visible, UV, X-rays and gamma rays

learn.hook: Your eyes see only a thin slice of the spectrum, from about 400 nm to 700 nm. Beyond violet lie rays that can disinfect water, image bones and treat cancer.
points: Visible light: about 700 nm (red) to 400 nm (violet). The eye is most sensitive near the middle (yellow-green). Some animals see beyond: honeybees see into the ultraviolet, and snakes can sense infrared.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): produced by the Sun and special lamps. Most solar UV is absorbed by the ozone layer. UV lamps sterilise water and instruments; precise UV lasers are used in LASIK eye surgery. Welders wear special glass goggles to protect eyes from UV.
X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): produced by bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons. Used for medical diagnosis and cancer treatment; overexposure damages tissue.
Gamma rays (below about 10⁻³ nm): produced in nuclear reactions and emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.
Higher frequency means higher photon energy, and generally more harmful to living tissue.

example.q: A radiation has wavelength 300 nm. Identify it and one use.

topics.title: EM spectrum: the full table and problem practice

learn.hook: One table summarises it all: from radio waves longer than a cricket pitch to gamma rays smaller than an atomic nucleus.
points: Radio (> 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in aerials; detected by receiver aerials.

Microwave (0.1 m to 1 mm): klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes; detected by point-contact diodes. Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): vibrating atoms and molecules; detected by thermopiles, bolometers, IR film.
Light (700 nm to 400 nm): electrons in atoms dropping to lower energy levels; detected by the eye, photocells, photographic film.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): inner shell electrons in atoms; detected by photocells and photographic film. X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): X-ray tubes or inner shell electrons; detected by photographic film, Geiger tubes, ionisation chambers.
Gamma rays (< 10⁻³ nm): radioactive decay of nuclei; detected the same way as X-rays. To identify a region, convert using c = νλ and compare with the ranges.

topics.title: Light rays and reflection by spherical mirrors

learn.hook: The dentist's small concave mirror and the convex mirror at a hilly hairpin bend in Uttarakhand obey the same two simple laws.
points: Light is electromagnetic radiation; the eye detects wavelengths from about 400 nm to 750 nm. Its speed in vacuum, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, is a fundamental constant.
Ray optics (geometrical optics): when the wavelength is tiny compared with the objects involved, light can be treated as travelling in straight lines called rays. A bundle of rays is a beam.
Laws of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
For a spherical mirror, the normal at any point is along the radius through that point (towards the centre of curvature).

Terms: pole P (centre of the mirror's surface), centre of curvature C, principal axis (line through P and C), aperture (size of the mirror). Paraxial rays are rays close to and nearly parallel to the principal axis.

example.q: A ray strikes a concave mirror at a point, making 25° with the radius drawn to that point. What is the angle of reflection?
steps: The radius is the normal at that point.
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence

learn.reallife: The convex mirrors fixed at sharp turns on mountain roads in Himachal Pradesh give drivers a wide view of oncoming traffic around the bend.

topics.title: Sign convention and the mirror equation

learn.hook: Mirror problems become simple arithmetic once you agree on one rule for signs. Physicists use the Cartesian sign convention, like a number line placed on the mirror's axis.
points: Cartesian sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive, against it negative; heights above the axis are positive, below negative.
With light coming from the left, the object distance u is negative for real objects. Focal length of a concave mirror is negative; of a convex mirror, positive.
Focal length f = R/2 for spherical mirrors (paraxial rays).
Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, derived from similar triangles in a ray diagram.
Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. Negative m means a real, inverted image; positive m means a virtual, erect image.

example.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image position and magnification.
example.answer: v = -60 cm (real, in front); m = -2 (inverted, twice the size)

learn.reallife: Shaving and make-up mirrors are concave: placed within f of your face, they give an enlarged, erect, virtual image, matching m positive and greater than 1.

points: Concave mirror, object beyond C: image between F and C, real, inverted, diminished.

Object at F: image at infinity. Object between F and P: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect, magnified.

learn.hook: A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looks bent at the surface. Light changes speed as it crosses from water to air, and that bends its path.
points: Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; and Snell's law: sin i/sin r = n₂₁ (a constant for the pair of media and a given colour).
Refractive index of medium 2 relative to 1: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂. Absolute refractive index n = c/v.
Going from rarer to denser (n₂₁ > 1), the ray bends towards the normal (r < i); from denser to rarer, it bends away from the normal.
Useful relations: n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁, and n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₁₂.
Typical refractive indices: air 1.0003, water 1.33, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42.

example.q: Light travels from air into glass of refractive index 1.5. Find its speed in glass.

learn.reallife: Diamonds cut in Surat, India's diamond capital, sparkle partly because diamond's high refractive index (2.42) bends light strongly.

topics.title: Slabs, apparent depth and total internal reflection

learn.hook: A swimming pool always looks shallower than it is, and on a hot road you see 'water' that is not there. Both tricks come from refraction near a boundary.
points: Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral shift), which grows with slab thickness and angle of incidence.
Apparent depth (for near-normal viewing) = real depth/n. A pool 2 m deep in water (n = 4/3) looks 1.5 m deep. The normal shift is d(1 - 1/n).
Going from a denser to a rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle ic, the refraction angle is 90°.
Total internal reflection (TIR) happens when light goes from denser to rarer medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds ic. Then all light is reflected.
sin ic = 1/n₂₁ (n of denser relative to rarer). Critical angles: water 48.75°, crown glass about 41°, diamond about 24.4°.

example.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a 12 cm deep beaker of water (n = 4/3). How deep does it appear, and by how much is it raised?
example.answer: Appears 9 cm deep; raised by 3 cm

learn.reallife: Mirages on the Delhi-Jaipur highway in May are caused by refraction and total internal reflection of skylight in hot, less dense air near the road surface.
